Mammals.Bat: The only mammals capable of true flight; their wings are stretched skin over elongated finger bones, and many navigate by echolocation.
Mammals.Whale: Whales breathe air, nurse their young on milk, and are warm-blooded. The blue whale is the largest animal known ever to have lived.
Mammals.Dolphin: Dolphins are mammals, not fish. They sleep with half the brain at a time, so they can keep surfacing to breathe.
Mammals.Platypus: One of the few egg-laying mammals. The male has a venomous spur on each hind leg, and the bill senses electric fields from prey.
Mammals.Echidna: A spiny egg-laying mammal, a monotreme like the platypus. Its egg hatches in a pouch, and the baby is called a puggle.
Mammals.Human: Humans are mammals too: warm-blooded, hairy, and milk-fed as babies. We are primates, closely related to chimpanzees and gorillas.
Mammals.Hedgehog: A hedgehog has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines, which are modified hairs. It rolls into a tight ball when threatened.
Mammals.Walrus: This mammal's tusks are long canine teeth, used to haul its heavy body onto ice and to break breathing holes.
Mammals.Manatee: Slow, gentle sea cows that eat seagrass all day. Despite their bulk, their closest living land relatives are elephants.
Mammals.Aardvark: The name is Afrikaans for earth pig, but it is no pig. It is the sole survivor of its own order and eats thousands of termites a night.
Mammals.Otter: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, and sometimes hold paws while sleeping.
Mammals.Shrew: Tiny, fast-living mammals. Some must eat nearly constantly because their hearts beat many hundreds of times a minute.
Mammals.Penguin: A bird, not a mammal. It cannot fly, but its wings have become flippers that propel it underwater like a fast swimmer.
Mammals.Shark: A fish whose skeleton is cartilage, not bone. Unlike mammals, sharks breathe through gills and are mostly cold-blooded.
Mammals.Lizard: Lizards are reptiles with scaly skin and lay eggs, though some species give birth to live young. None produce milk.
Mammals.Ostrich: The largest living bird, standing about 2.5 metres tall. It is a bird with feathers and lays eggs, so not a mammal.
Mammals.Salamander: An amphibian that looks like a lizard but has moist, scaleless skin. Some species can regrow lost limbs.
Mammals.Frog: Amphibians that lay eggs in water. Their tadpoles breathe with gills before growing lungs and legs.
Mammals.Crocodile: A reptile that has barely changed in millions of years. It lays eggs and is cold-blooded, unlike any mammal.
Mammals.Eel: A snake-shaped fish, not a mammal. European eels are born in the Sargasso Sea and travel thousands of kilometres to rivers.
Mammals.Tuna: A powerful fish that is partly warm-blooded, which is unusual for fish. It still breathes through gills, so it is no mammal.
Mammals.Turtle: A reptile that lays eggs on land. Its shell is part of its skeleton, fused to the ribs and spine.
Mammals.Emu: A huge flightless Australian bird. Like the ostrich it lays eggs and has feathers, so it is not a mammal.
Mammals.Octopus: A mollusc with three hearts and blue blood. It is intelligent, but it is an invertebrate, nowhere near a mammal.

Plants that grow in water.Water lily: The water lily floats its pads and flowers on the surface. The giant Amazon one, Victoria, bears leaves strong enough to hold a small child.
Plants that grow in water.Lotus: The lotus rises from muddy water, with leaves that repel it, an effect called the lotus effect. Its seeds can stay viable for centuries.
Plants that grow in water.Duckweed: Duckweed is among the smallest flowering plants, and doubles in number within days. It's studied as a source of protein and for cleaning wastewater.
Plants that grow in water.Cattail: Cattails grow in marshes, with brown, sausage-like seed heads. Their roots, shoots and pollen are all edible.
Plants that grow in water.Water hyacinth: The water hyacinth is pretty but a notorious invader. It can cover lakes in dense mats, and it doubles its coverage in as little as two weeks.
Plants that grow in water.Seagrass: Seagrass is a true flowering plant that lives underwater. Its meadows store carbon very efficiently, and shelter young fish.
Plants that grow in water.Papyrus: Papyrus is a tall sedge of the Nile. Ancient Egyptians made it into paper-like writing sheets, from which the word paper comes.
Plants that grow in water.Watercress: Watercress grows in cool, flowing streams. It's one of the oldest cultivated leaf vegetables, and tastes peppery.
Plants that grow in water.Mangrove: Mangroves are trees that tolerate salt water, with tangled roots that rise above the mud. They shield coasts from storms.
Plants that grow in water.Reed: Reeds grow in shallow water and wetlands. Common reed is used for thatched roofs, which can last about 50 years.
Plants that grow in water.Pondweed: Pondweed grows submerged in lakes and ponds, with only flowers reaching the surface. Fish and waterfowl rely on it.
Plants that grow in water.Wild rice: Wild rice is a water grass native to North America, and not related to common rice. Its grains are harvested from canoes by Indigenous people in the Great Lakes.
Plants that grow in water.Cactus: Cacti store water in thick stems and thrive in dry soil. Most live only in the Americas, excepting a single species in Africa.
Plants that grow in water.Lavender: Lavender prefers dry, sunny, well-drained soil, and rots in waterlogged ground. This makes it a Mediterranean hillside plant, not a pond one.
Plants that grow in water.Sunflower: Sunflowers need full sun and well-drained soil. Young sunflower heads track the sun across the sky, a behaviour called heliotropism.
Plants that grow in water.Oak: Oaks are land trees, usually not water-tolerant. Some, like the pin oak, can cope with wet ground, but not underwater living.
Plants that grow in water.Rosemary: Rosemary is a Mediterranean shrub preferring dry soil. Its name means 'dew of the sea' in Latin.
Plants that grow in water.Agave: Agave stores water in thick leaves and thrives in arid land. Tequila is made from the blue agave's roasted heart.
Plants that grow in water.Edelweiss: Edelweiss grows on rocky mountain slopes in the Alps. Its woolly hairs shield it from cold and strong ultraviolet light.
Plants that grow in water.Heather: Heather grows on dry, acidic moorland. It's a food source for grouse, and honey from its flowers is dark and jelly-like.
Plants that grow in water.Aloe: Aloe stores gel in fleshy leaves, an adaptation to dry climates. It's one of the oldest known medicinal plants.
Plants that grow in water.Pine: Pines are land conifers, usually in dry or poor soil. Bristlecone pines, found at high altitude, are among the longest-lived trees.
Plants that grow in water.Sagebrush: Sagebrush covers dry western North American plains. It gives the region its distinctive scent after rain.
Plants that grow in water.Tumbleweed: Tumbleweed is a dry plant that breaks off and rolls across the desert, spreading seeds. The common one is the invasive Russian thistle.

Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Mercury: Mercury is the smallest planet, yet its year lasts only 88 days, and its shadowed polar craters hold ice.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Venus: Venus is hotter than Mercury, around 465 degrees Celsius, and its day is longer than its year.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Earth: Earth is the only planet known to have life, and the only one not named for a god.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Mars: Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system at about 22 km, roughly 2.5 times higher than Everest.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Jupiter: Jupiter holds more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined, and its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Saturn: Saturn is less dense than water, so a bathtub big enough would let it float.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Uranus: Uranus is tipped about 98 degrees, so it rolls around the Sun on its side.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Neptune: Neptune was found in 1846 by calculation before anyone saw it, and one of its years lasts about 165 Earth years.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Pluto: Pluto was demoted to dwarf planet in 2006; it was named in 1930 by an 11-year-old girl in England, Venetia Burney.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Ceres: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system, visited by the Dawn probe.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Eris: Eris, found in 2005, is about as big as Pluto but more massive, and its discovery triggered Pluto's demotion.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Makemake: Makemake is named for the creator god of Easter Island's Rapa Nui people, and it was found in 2005.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Haumea: Haumea is a fast-spinning, football-shaped dwarf planet with a day under four hours, a ring and two moons.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.The Moon: The Moon orbits Earth, so it's a moon and not a planet, though it's bigger than Pluto.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Titan: Titan is a moon of Saturn bigger than Mercury, with a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Europa: Europa is a moon of Jupiter, with an ice shell over a salty ocean, so it's a moon and not a planet.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Ganymede: Ganymede is the solar system's largest moon, bigger than Mercury, but it still orbits Jupiter.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Io: Io is Jupiter's volcanic moon, the most volcanically active body known.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Callisto: Callisto is a heavily cratered moon of Jupiter, not a planet.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.The Sun: The Sun is a star, holding 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Halley's Comet: Halley's Comet is an icy body that returns every 76 years or so, and a comet isn't a planet.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Vesta: Vesta is a big asteroid in the belt visited by the Dawn probe; it falls just short of dwarf-planet status.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Charon: Charon is Pluto's largest moon, so large that the two orbit a point in space between them.
Planets or dwarf planets of our solar sy.Triton: Triton is Neptune's largest moon and orbits backward, probably a captured Kuiper Belt object.

Things that are actually stars.Sirius: Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky, only about 8.6 light-years away.
Things that are actually stars.Polaris: Polaris isn't the brightest star; it's famous for sitting near the north celestial pole.
Things that are actually stars.Betelgeuse: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in Orion that dimmed in 2019 and 2020 in the Great Dimming.
Things that are actually stars.Rigel: Rigel is a blue supergiant in Orion, over a hundred thousand times as luminous as the Sun.
Things that are actually stars.Vega: Vega was the north star about 12,000 years ago and will be again in about 13,000 years.
Things that are actually stars.Arcturus: Arcturus is an orange giant, and the story goes that its light opened the 1933 Chicago World's Fair.
Things that are actually stars.Aldebaran: Aldebaran is the red eye of Taurus, and the Pioneer 10 spacecraft is roughly headed in its direction.
Things that are actually stars.Antares: Antares is a red supergiant so huge that it would engulf Mars' orbit if it replaced the Sun.
Things that are actually stars.Proxima Centauri: Proxima Centauri is the closest star to the Sun, 4.2 light-years away, a red dwarf too faint to see unaided.
Things that are actually stars.Deneb: Deneb is one of the most luminous stars visible, more than a thousand light-years away.
Things that are actually stars.Altair: Altair spins once in about nine hours, so fast it is flattened.
Things that are actually stars.Canopus: Canopus is the second-brightest star in the night sky and is used by spacecraft to navigate.
Things that are actually stars.The Sun: The Sun is an ordinary yellow dwarf star, and it holds 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass.
Things that are actually stars.Orion: Orion is a constellation, a pattern of stars rather than a star.
Things that are actually stars.Andromeda: Andromeda is a constellation and the name of a nearby galaxy, not a star.
Things that are actually stars.Pleiades: The Pleiades is a cluster of hot young stars, not a single star.
Things that are actually stars.Halley's Comet: Halley's Comet is an icy body that glows only from sunlight, not a star.
Things that are actually stars.Jupiter: Jupiter is a planet, which shines by reflecting sunlight.
Things that are actually stars.Venus: Venus is often called the 'morning star' or 'evening star', but it's a planet.
Things that are actually stars.Ganymede: Ganymede is a moon of Jupiter, not a star.
Things that are actually stars.Milky Way: The Milky Way is a galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars, not a star.
Things that are actually stars.Crab Nebula: The Crab Nebula is a cloud of gas left behind when a star exploded, not a star.
Things that are actually stars.Titan: Titan is Saturn's moon, bigger than Mercury, with a thick atmosphere and methane lakes; it shines by reflected light, not as a star.
Things that are actually stars.Ceres: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, holding about a third of the belt's mass, but it is a rocky, icy world, not a star.

Things that float in water.Cork: Bark of the cork oak, about half air-filled cells, so it floats well; it was used on fishing nets and life vests for centuries.
Things that float in water.Ice cube: Water is rare in that its solid form is less dense than its liquid, as it expands about 9 percent on freezing, so ice floats.
Things that float in water.Rubber duck: The air inside and the light plastic keep it up, and a 1992 cargo spill sent 28,800 toys across the oceans, helping track currents.
Things that float in water.Beach ball: Mostly air in a thin skin, so it's very light for its size, and it floats by displacing lots of water.
Things that float in water.Styrofoam: Expanded polystyrene is about 98 percent air, making it so buoyant that it is used in docks and lifebuoys.
Things that float in water.Pumice: A volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles that it floats, and rafts of it have drifted across the Pacific for years.
Things that float in water.Apple: Apples are about 25 percent air, which is why they bob, and why apple bobbing is a Halloween party game.
Things that float in water.Coconut: Coconuts float thanks to their husk and air pockets, and that lets them colonize far-off islands by ocean drift.
Things that float in water.Ping pong ball: Hollow and light, so it floats high, and it takes a lot of pushing to hold it under water.
Things that float in water.Olive oil: Oil is less dense than water, about 0.9 times, so it floats on top, and that's why oil spills spread across the sea's surface.
Things that float in water.Dry leaf: A leaf's thin, light body and its waxy surface let it ride on the surface tension of water.
Things that float in water.Rock: A trap: most rocks are about three times denser than water, so they sink, though pumice is the exception that floats.
Things that float in water.Coin: A trap: metal is denser than water, so it sinks, though a coin laid flat can very carefully rest on the surface tension.
Things that float in water.Iron nail: A trap: a nail is much denser than water, so it sinks, although an iron ship floats since its hull encloses air.
Things that float in water.Marble: A trap: glass or stone marbles are denser than water, so they sink straight to the bottom.
Things that float in water.Key: A trap: metal keys are dense, and sink, which is why people attach them to floating keychains at the beach.
Things that float in water.Honey: A trap: it is about 1.4 times as dense as water, so a drop sinks, and it dissolves slowly instead of mixing quickly.
Things that float in water.Golf ball: A trap: it is solid and denser than water, so it sinks, which is why lakes near golf courses are full of lost balls.
Things that float in water.Brick: A trap: a solid clay brick sinks, though some very porous bricks are famous for floating in marketing displays.
Things that float in water.Steel spoon: A trap: steel is nearly eight times denser than water, so it sinks, unlike a steel ship with a hollow hull.
Things that float in water.Lead weight: A trap: lead is about 11 times denser than water, which is why it's used in fishing sinkers.
Things that float in water.Anchor: A trap: that's literally its job; its dense metal and shape make it sink and grip the seabed.
Things that float in water.Diamond: A trap: diamond is about 3.5 times denser than water, so it sinks right away.
Things that float in water.Gold bar: A trap: gold is about 19 times denser than water, and that great density is how prospectors panned it from sand.

Black hole terminology.Event horizon: The boundary beyond which not even light can escape. For a black hole the size of the Sun, it would be only about 6 kilometers across.
Black hole terminology.Singularity: The point at the center, where current physics says density becomes infinite. Most physicists think it signals that our theory breaks down there.
Black hole terminology.Accretion disk: A swirling disk of hot gas spiralling into a black hole. Friction heats it enough to shine brilliantly in X-rays, which is how many black holes are found.
Black hole terminology.Photon sphere: A region where gravity is so strong that light can orbit the black hole. Around a non-spinning hole it sits 1.5 times the horizon radius out.
Black hole terminology.Hawking radiation: Stephen Hawking predicted in 1974 that black holes slowly leak radiation and may eventually evaporate. It hasn't been observed directly.
Black hole terminology.Ergosphere: Around a spinning black hole, space itself is dragged around so fast that nothing can stay still. It's the region just outside the event horizon.
Black hole terminology.Spaghettification: Tidal forces stretch anything falling in, pulling it into a long thin strand. The pull on your feet would greatly exceed that on your head.
Black hole terminology.Schwarzschild radius: The radius at which a mass becomes a black hole. Karl Schwarzschild worked it out in 1916, just weeks after Einstein published general relativity.
Black hole terminology.Quasar: The extremely bright core of a distant galaxy, powered by a supermassive black hole feeding on gas. Some outshine a whole galaxy of stars.
Black hole terminology.Photosynthesis: Plants making sugar from light, which is biology and not astrophysics. Black holes, on the other hand, give out almost no light of their own.
Black hole terminology.Continental drift: Alfred Wegener's idea of moving continents belongs to geology. It has nothing to do with black holes.
Black hole terminology.Mitochondria: The powerhouses of cells, a biology term. No relation to the cosmic dark.
Black hole terminology.Photosphere: The Sun's visible surface, about 5,500 degrees Celsius. A trap, since it sounds similar to photon sphere, but it's about stars, not black holes.
Black hole terminology.Solar wind: A stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. It causes auroras on Earth but is a solar term, not a black hole one.
Black hole terminology.Sunspot: A cooler, darker patch on the Sun's surface caused by magnetic activity. It belongs with our star, not black holes.
Black hole terminology.Solar flare: A sudden burst of energy from the Sun. It can disrupt radio and satellites, but it's a solar event.
Black hole terminology.Chromosphere: The thin red layer just above the Sun's visible surface. It's visible during a total eclipse, and it's a solar layer.
Black hole terminology.Asteroid belt: A region between Mars and Jupiter full of rocky debris. It's part of our solar system, not black hole vocabulary.
Black hole terminology.Kuiper Belt: A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto. It's a solar system structure, unrelated to black holes.
Black hole terminology.Comet tail: It forms when sunlight heats a comet's ice and blows the gas away, so the tail always points away from the Sun.
Black hole terminology.Lunar eclipse: It happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It belongs to Earth-Moon geometry, not black holes.
Black hole terminology.Ozone layer: A high-altitude shield that absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light. It's an atmospheric term.
Black hole terminology.Tectonic plate: A huge slab of Earth's crust that moves slowly. It's geology, nowhere near a black hole.
Black hole terminology.Trade winds: Steady easterly winds near the tropics that sailors used for centuries. They're weather, not black hole terms.

Fictional planets.Tatooine: Luke's desert home was named after Tataouine in Tunisia, where scenes were filmed in the real desert.
Fictional planets.Vulcan: Spock's home in Star Trek; 19th-century astronomers once hunted for a real planet called Vulcan inside Mercury's orbit, and it did not exist.
Fictional planets.Krypton: Superman's birth world, which exploded; the name came from the real element krypton, found in 1898, long before the comics.
Fictional planets.Arrakis: The desert planet in Dune, the only source of the 'spice', and home of enormous sandworms.
Fictional planets.Gallifrey: Home of Doctor Who's Time Lords, who in the story destroyed it during the Time War.
Fictional planets.Hoth: The ice planet in The Empire Strikes Back was filmed in Norway, near the Hardangerjøkulen glacier.
Fictional planets.Naboo: Home of Padmé Amidala in The Phantom Menace, and its royal palace was filmed at the Royal Palace of Caserta, Italy.
Fictional planets.Coruscant: A planet covered by one city, from Latin for 'to glitter', and seat of both the Republic and the Empire.
Fictional planets.Magrathea: In The Hitchhiker's Guide, it is a planet where custom planets are built, and its designer Slartibartfast won an award for Norway's fjords.
Fictional planets.Cybertron: Home of the Transformers, a metallic world torn by the war between Autobots and Decepticons.
Fictional planets.Dagobah: The swamp world where Yoda hid in exile, built on a studio set because the mist and mud had to be controlled.
Fictional planets.Kepler-22b: A real planet found in 2011 about 600 light-years away, in its star's habitable zone, so it is not fiction.
Fictional planets.Proxima b: A real planet orbiting Proxima Centauri, our nearest neighbour star, only about 4.2 light-years away; found in 2016.
Fictional planets.TRAPPIST-1e: A real Earth-sized planet, one of seven circling a small red star about 40 light-years away.
Fictional planets.51 Pegasi b: A real planet, the first found orbiting a Sun-like star, in 1995, which earned a Nobel Prize in 2019.
Fictional planets.Eris: A real dwarf planet whose 2005 discovery helped lead to Pluto's demotion; it is named for the Greek goddess of discord.
Fictional planets.Makemake: A real dwarf planet named for the creator god of Easter Island's Rapa Nui people, found around Easter 2005.
Fictional planets.Haumea: A real egg-shaped dwarf planet that spins in under four hours and has a ring.
Fictional planets.Sedna: A real remote world whose orbit takes about 11,000 years.
Fictional planets.Ceres: A real dwarf planet and the largest object in the asteroid belt; the Dawn probe visited in 2015.
Fictional planets.Quaoar: A real icy world in the Kuiper belt; in 2023 astronomers found its ring lies much farther out than expected.
Fictional planets.Gliese 581c: A real exoplanet announced in 2007 as potentially habitable, a hope later shot down by other findings.
Fictional planets.Arrokoth: A real snowman-shaped Kuiper belt object that New Horizons flew past on 1 January 2019.
Fictional planets.Charon: Pluto's largest moon is so big the two orbit a point between them, but it is a real moon, not a fictional world.

Computer science pioneers.Alan Turing: Defined what a computer can compute, cracked Enigma at Bletchley Park, and gave the world the Turing test.
Computer science pioneers.Ada Lovelace: In 1843 she wrote what is often called the first computer program, for Babbage's machine, and she was Lord Byron's daughter.
Computer science pioneers.Charles Babbage: He designed the Difference Engine and Analytical Engine; the Science Museum built his Difference Engine No. 2 from his plans in 1991, and it worked.
Computer science pioneers.Grace Hopper: A US Navy rear admiral who pioneered compilers, and she is linked to the famous 1947 moth found in Harvard's Mark II computer.
Computer science pioneers.John von Neumann: His stored-program design still sits behind most computers, and he also worked on the Manhattan Project and game theory.
Computer science pioneers.Tim Berners-Lee: He proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 at CERN, and he chose not to patent it.
Computer science pioneers.Claude Shannon: Founded information theory in 1948, and his master's thesis showed that Boolean logic could design circuits.
Computer science pioneers.Dennis Ritchie: He created the C language and co-created Unix at Bell Labs, and he died in 2011, a week after Steve Jobs.
Computer science pioneers.Linus Torvalds: Started Linux as a hobby project in 1991, and then built Git in 2005.
Computer science pioneers.Margaret Hamilton: Led the Apollo onboard flight software team; her code's priority system kept the Apollo 11 landing alive during an alarm.
Computer science pioneers.Donald Knuth: Author of The Art of Computer Programming and creator of TeX, who sends cheques for errors readers find.
Computer science pioneers.Isaac Newton: Gave us gravity and calculus, not computers; his rival Leibniz laid early groundwork for binary arithmetic, which every computer uses.
Computer science pioneers.Charles Darwin: Evolution by natural selection in 1859, whose ideas now inspire genetic algorithms in computer science, but he was a biologist.
Computer science pioneers.Gregor Mendel: A friar who bred pea plants and founded genetics, and his work was ignored until about 1900.
Computer science pioneers.Louis Pasteur: A chemist famed for pasteurisation and vaccines, including the rabies vaccine of 1885.
Computer science pioneers.Marie Curie: Won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry; her notebooks are still radioactive today.
Computer science pioneers.Nikola Tesla: Engineer behind alternating-current power, and the unit of magnetic field is named after him.
Computer science pioneers.Thomas Edison: The inventor held about 1,000 US patents, but computing was not one of them.
Computer science pioneers.Carl Sagan: An astronomer and science communicator, co-creator of the Voyager Golden Record.
Computer science pioneers.Neil Armstrong: Another trap: Armstrong flew to the Moon, steered by the Apollo Guidance Computer built by Hamilton's team.
Computer science pioneers.Edwin Hubble: Showed in the 1920s that Andromeda is a separate galaxy, and the space telescope bears his name.
Computer science pioneers.Jane Goodall: Studied chimpanzees, and in 1960 discovered that they make and use tools.
Computer science pioneers.Albert Einstein: Won the 1921 Nobel for the photoelectric effect, which underlies digital camera sensors, but he was no computer pioneer.
Computer science pioneers.Max Planck: His quantum theory of 1900 gave us Planck's constant, which since 2019 defines the kilogram.

Things you can tune.Piano: A piano has over 200 strings, and their combined tension is around 20 tons, which is why tuners need strong pins.
Things you can tune.Guitar: Standard tuning is E-A-D-G-B-E, and many players retune strings to open tunings for slide or folk music.
Things you can tune.Violin: The four strings are tuned in perfect fifths, G-D-A-E, a pattern that violin makers have used for centuries.
Things you can tune.Radio: On older sets and radios, you tune a dial until the signal locks in, and the phrase tune in is still used today.
Things you can tune.Car engine: A mechanic can tune ignition timing and fuel mix, which is why a tuned engine feels livelier.
Things you can tune.Timpani: It's one of the only drums with a definite pitch, changed by pedals that adjust the head's tension.
Things you can tune.Harp: A concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals, and the player tunes its colored strings in sequence, C red, F black.
Things you can tune.Television: Analog sets were tuned with a dial or knob to find each channel, and the habit lives on in 'stay tuned'.
Things you can tune.Snare drum: Drummers adjust the tension rods to tune the head and the wires underneath, shaping its crack.
Things you can tune.Ukulele: A ukulele is usually tuned G-C-E-A, with a high G string that gives it its sunny, re-entrant sound.
Things you can tune.Bicycle: Cyclists tune up a bike by adjusting gears and brakes, an everyday use of the word.
Things you can tune.Triangle: A triangle makes a high, ringing sound with no definite pitch, so there's nothing to tune.
Things you can tune.Maracas: Maracas are rattles filled with seeds or beads, once made from dried gourds, and not tuned to a pitch.
Things you can tune.Cymbal: Zildjian, a cymbal maker founded in Istanbul in 1623, makes bronze plates that crash and shimmer but aren't tuned.
Things you can tune.Castanets: Castanets are named from the Spanish word for chestnut, and their click has no definite pitch.
Things you can tune.Sandwich: A sandwich is named for the Earl of Sandwich, and has no tuning pegs, only layers.
Things you can tune.Pillow: A pillow can be fluffed or squashed, but there is nothing to tune, only to plump.
Things you can tune.Cloud: A fluffy cumulus cloud can weigh around 500 tonnes, but you can't tune it.
Things you can tune.Spoon: Spoons are older than forks by thousands of years; nobody tunes one, though people play them as percussion.
Things you can tune.Shoe: You can polish a shoe or lace it up, but nothing about it can be tuned.
Things you can tune.Banana: A banana is slightly radioactive from potassium-40, but there's no tuning it.
Things you can tune.Book: A book can be opened, bound or read, but not tuned, unless it's a songbook.
Things you can tune.Carpet: A carpet can be woven, beaten or cleaned, but there's nothing to tune.
Things you can tune.Kazoo: A kazoo has no tuning: the pitch comes from the player's voice, which buzzes a thin membrane.

Martial arts.Karate: Karate began in Okinawa and means empty hand; it was added to the Olympics for Tokyo 2020 only, and it was dropped again for Paris.
Martial arts.Judo: Judo means the gentle way, and it was created in 1882 by Jigoro Kano, who made it the first Asian martial art in the Olympics, in 1964.
Martial arts.Taekwondo: Taekwondo is Korea's national sport, and its high, fast kicks are the core of the art; it joined the Olympics in 2000 as a full medal sport.
Martial arts.Kung fu: Kung fu is an umbrella term for hundreds of Chinese styles, and in Chinese it originally meant skill from effort, not fighting.
Martial arts.Aikido: Aikido was developed by Morihei Ueshiba, and its techniques redirect an attacker's force rather than meet it head-on.
Martial arts.Jiu-jitsu: Jiu-jitsu's Brazilian form was built by the Gracie family from Japanese judo, and it is known for ground fighting and submissions.
Martial arts.Muay Thai: Muay Thai is Thailand's national sport, known as the art of eight limbs because it uses fists, elbows, knees and shins.
Martial arts.Capoeira: Capoeira was developed by enslaved Africans in Brazil, and its fighting moves are disguised as dance and music.
Martial arts.Krav Maga: Krav Maga was developed in the 1930s by Imi Lichtenfeld and became the hand-to-hand system of the Israeli military.
Martial arts.Kendo: Kendo is Japanese fencing with bamboo swords and body armor, and it grew out of the samurai's sword training.
Martial arts.Wing Chun: Wing Chun is a close-range Chinese style, and Bruce Lee studied it under Ip Man before founding his own approach.
Martial arts.Tai chi: Tai chi looks like slow dance, but it began as a martial art and is now most practiced for balance and calm.
Martial arts.Sumo: Sumo is Japan's ancient wrestling, and the sport's top rank, yokozuna, is held for life, though the rikishi must retire when they stop winning.
Martial arts.Origami: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding, not a fighting art, and some designs use no cuts or glue at all.
Martial arts.Ikebana: Ikebana is Japanese flower arranging that stresses line and empty space, and some schools date back to the 15th century.
Martial arts.Bonsai: Bonsai is the art of growing miniature trees in containers, and some are centuries old; it's Japanese, not martial.
Martial arts.Haiku: A haiku is a 5-7-5 syllable poem from Japan, and it focuses on a seasonal image, not combat.
Martial arts.Karaoke: Karaoke is Japanese for empty orchestra, and Daisuke Inoue's 1971 machine started the craze; it's entertainment, not combat.
Martial arts.Sudoku: Sudoku is a number puzzle, and the name is short for a Japanese phrase meaning the digits must remain single.
Martial arts.Kabuki: Kabuki is a stylized Japanese theater with dramatic makeup, and while it includes stage fights, it is a performance, not a fighting art.
Martial arts.Feng shui: Feng shui is the Chinese practice of arranging space for harmony; it's about layout, not fighting.
Martial arts.Pilates: Pilates was created by Joseph Pilates, a German, to rehabilitate people, and it is a fitness method rather than a martial art.
Martial arts.Zumba: Zumba is a Colombian-born dance fitness craze created by Alberto Perez in the 1990s; it has dance moves, not combat.
Martial arts.Yoga: Yoga is an ancient Indian discipline of posture, breath and meditation, and it is not a martial art despite its strength demands.

Things that melt.Butter: Butter melts at around 32 to 35 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why it feels so smooth on the tongue.
Things that melt.Ice cube: An ice cube melts in your drink because the liquid warms it up, and it takes in a lot of energy, which is why it chills so well.
Things that melt.Candle wax: Paraffin wax melts at about 50 to 60 degrees Celsius, and a candle burns the vapor from melted wax rather than the solid.
Things that melt.Chocolate: Cocoa butter melts close to body temperature, which is why chocolate melts in your mouth but stays solid on the shelf.
Things that melt.Crayon: A crayon is mostly paraffin wax with pigment, and it will soften and melt in a hot car.
Things that melt.Ice cream: Ice cream melts fast because it is a mix of ice crystals, fat, and air, and stabilizers slow the process down.
Things that melt.Snowman: A snowman melts as the snow absorbs heat from the air and sun, and the packed snow lasts longer than loose powder.
Things that melt.Cheese: Cheeses like mozzarella melt well because of their moisture and protein, while halloumi has a high melting point, so it grills.
Things that melt.Popsicle: The Popsicle was reportedly invented in 1905 by an 11-year-old, Frank Epperson, who left soda and a stick out overnight.
Things that melt.Hot glue stick: A hot glue stick is a plastic that melts at roughly 120 degrees Celsius in the gun, then hardens again when it cools.
Things that melt.Marshmallow: Marshmallows melt because their sugar and gelatin soften with heat, and toasting one makes the outside brown and the inside gooey.
Things that melt.Wood: Wood doesn't melt, it burns or chars. Heat breaks the material down into ash and gases before it can turn to liquid.
Things that melt.Paper: Paper doesn't melt but burns, and Fahrenheit 451, the title of Bradbury's novel, is roughly the temperature where it ignites.
Things that melt.Bread: Bread doesn't melt; heat just dries and browns it, and toasting is a chemical change called the Maillard reaction.
Things that melt.Cotton: Cotton does not melt, but burns, unlike synthetic fabrics, which melt and stick to skin.
Things that melt.Stone: Rock does melt, but only at extreme heat, and it takes over 700 degrees Celsius to turn into magma.
Things that melt.Feather: A feather is made of keratin, the same protein as your hair, and it burns or chars rather than melts.
Things that melt.Popcorn: Popcorn does not melt; the kernel pops when water inside turns to steam and bursts the hull.
Things that melt.Sponge: A natural sponge is an animal skeleton, and it doesn't melt, though a plastic one might in extreme heat.
Things that melt.Brick: Bricks are fired in a kiln at over 1,000 degrees Celsius, so they won't melt in any ordinary fire.
Things that melt.Leather: Leather doesn't melt but dries, stiffens, and chars when heated.
Things that melt.Rice: Rice doesn't melt but softens as its starch absorbs water, and it will burn if heated dry.
Things that melt.Cardboard: Cardboard burns rather than melts, and its layered paper fibers decompose with heat.
Things that melt.Wool: Wool resists fire better than most fabrics because it holds a lot of moisture and chars, and it does not melt.

Things for wrapping a present.Wrapping paper: Wrapping paper took off after 1917, when a Kansas store ran out of tissue and sold decorated envelope liners.
Things for wrapping a present.Ribbon: Curling ribbon curls when you pull it sharply along a blade's edge, which stretches one side of the ribbon.
Things for wrapping a present.Bow: The bow's loops are made from pulled ribbon, and it's often the most expensive part of a wrapped gift.
Things for wrapping a present.Gift tag: A tag is where the 'to' and 'from' go, and some gift tags double as ornaments the recipient can keep.
Things for wrapping a present.Sticky tape: Cellophane tape was invented by 3M's Richard Drew in 1930, and it became popular during the Depression for mending.
Things for wrapping a present.Tissue paper: Tissue paper is so thin and light that a single sheet is often less than a tenth of a millimeter.
Things for wrapping a present.Gift bag: The gift bag took off in the 1980s and 90s as an easier alternative that you can reuse.
Things for wrapping a present.Scissors: Scissors date back over 3,000 years, and the pivoted modern design has been around since Roman times.
Things for wrapping a present.Gift box: A box makes wrapping odd shapes easier, and a boxed present hides its contents better than a loose one.
Things for wrapping a present.Twine: Twine is plain string made from twisted fibers, often jute, a natural look that's popular for rustic wrapping.
Things for wrapping a present.Curling ribbon: Running a ribbon along scissors blades makes it curl, and it's a common finishing touch on balloons too.
Things for wrapping a present.Spatula: A spatula is for flipping and spreading, not wrapping, though it can help smooth icing on a cake.
Things for wrapping a present.Hammer: Wrapping a present needs no hammer, but one is a classic 'hard to wrap' gift: odd shapes are why people reach for bags and boxes.
Things for wrapping a present.Paintbrush: A paintbrush is for paint, though you can use one to apply glue to a craft project.
Things for wrapping a present.Sponge: Natural sponge is actually an animal, and a wet sponge can dampen the glue on an envelope or stamp.
Things for wrapping a present.Whisk: A balloon whisk's wires are shaped to trap air as you beat, which is why meringue gets so fluffy.
Things for wrapping a present.Colander: Italian cooks drain pasta in a colander, and the holes also let steam escape so noodles don't go soggy.
Things for wrapping a present.Plunger: A plunger works by pushing air and water, and the flat-rim type is for sinks while the flanged type is for toilets.
Things for wrapping a present.Ladle: A ladle's long handle keeps your hand away from hot soup, and the bowl is sized to hold about one serving.
Things for wrapping a present.Toothbrush: Bristles on early toothbrushes came from boar hair, in a design traced to 15th-century China.
Things for wrapping a present.Mop: The word mop dates to the 1400s, and the first modern 'self-wringing' mop was patented by Thomas Stewart in 1893.
Things for wrapping a present.Pliers: Pliers multiply your grip with a lever, and the same design principle appears in scissors and nutcrackers.
Things for wrapping a present.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, though it could smooth out creased paper in a pinch.
Things for wrapping a present.Funnel: Funnels have been used since ancient times, and a wide cone feeding a narrow neck stops spills when pouring.

Things with a buckle.Belt: A belt's buckle has a prong that slips into a hole, and the design is ancient: Roman soldiers used metal buckles on their gear.
Things with a buckle.Seatbelt: A seatbelt buckle can be released with a push of a button, and the three-point belt was invented by Volvo in 1959.
Things with a buckle.Dog collar: A dog collar has a buckle or snap, and the oldest ones were spiked iron collars to protect hunting dogs from wolves.
Things with a buckle.Baby car seat: A car seat's harness buckle must be snug, and safety experts suggest you shouldn't be able to pinch the strap at the shoulder.
Things with a buckle.Watch strap: A watch strap's buckle is like a belt's, and it allows adjustment, which is why leather bands have little holes.
Things with a buckle.Life jacket: A life jacket's buckles keep it from slipping off, and it's required for every person on boats in many places.
Things with a buckle.Ski boot: Ski boots use buckles because they give tight, adjustable support, and modern ones can be clamped with a micro-adjusting lever.
Things with a buckle.Pilgrim hat: The buckle on the pilgrim hat is a myth: historians say Pilgrims rarely wore buckles, which were popularized in the 1800s.
Things with a buckle.Backpack: A backpack's chest and hip buckles spread the load across the body, and the clips are usually quick-release plastic.
Things with a buckle.Overalls: Overalls have metal buckles at the shoulder straps, which allows the length to be adjusted, and they became workwear in the 1800s.
Things with a buckle.Necktie: A necktie has no buckle, and its knot holds it in place, with the classic four-in-hand being the common one.
Things with a buckle.Sock: A sock has no buckle at all, and it's held up by elastic, which in the past was done with garters.
Things with a buckle.Sneaker: A sneaker usually has laces or Velcro, and although some have buckles, it's not the usual fastener.
Things with a buckle.Scarf: A scarf is only wrapped or knotted around the neck, with no buckle needed.
Things with a buckle.Glove: A glove might have a wrist strap, but standard ones don't have buckles, and they're pulled on by hand.
Things with a buckle.T-shirt: A T-shirt has no fasteners at all, and it got its name from the T-shape of the body and sleeves.
Things with a buckle.Hoodie: A hoodie has a drawstring and a zipper or no closure, and it's not typically fastened with a buckle.
Things with a buckle.Flip-flop: A flip-flop has a thong strap with no fastening, and its name comes from the sound it makes when you walk.
Things with a buckle.Beanie: A beanie is just a knit cap, with no fasteners, and the name might come from 'bean', slang for head.
Things with a buckle.Slipper: A slipper slides on without any fastening, which is the whole point of it.
Things with a buckle.Wellington boot: A wellington is a waterproof pull-on boot named after the Duke of Wellington, and it has no buckle.
Things with a buckle.Bath towel: A bath towel is a plain piece of terry cloth, which is made of looped threads for absorbency, and no buckle.
Things with a buckle.Pillowcase: A pillowcase has an open end that slips over the pillow, so it needs no buckle or fastener.
Things with a buckle.Mitten: A mitten is a one-piece hand cover with no buckle, and some come with a cord or clip to avoid losing them.

Things with wings that can't fly.Penguin: Penguins use their wings as flippers, and they 'fly' through water at speeds of up to about 35 kilometers an hour in the case of gentoos.
Things with wings that can't fly.Ostrich: Ostriches are the largest living birds, up to about 2.7 meters tall, and they use their wings for balance while running at around 70 km/h.
Things with wings that can't fly.Emu: Emus are flightless birds from Australia, and their wings are tiny, only about 20 centimeters long.
Things with wings that can't fly.Kiwi: Kiwis have wings so tiny they're nearly invisible under their shaggy feathers, and females lay an egg that's about a fifth of her weight.
Things with wings that can't fly.Dodo: The dodo was a flightless bird from Mauritius, and it was extinct within about a century of sailors' arrival around 1600.
Things with wings that can't fly.Cassowary: The cassowary has a helmet-like casque, and its wings are small, but its legs have a dagger-like claw that can be dangerous.
Things with wings that can't fly.Kakapo: The kakapo is a flightless, nocturnal parrot of New Zealand, and it's critically endangered, with only about 250 alive.
Things with wings that can't fly.Rhea: Rheas are South American flightless birds that use their wings like sails to turn quickly when running.
Things with wings that can't fly.Buffalo wing: A trap: buffalo wings are chicken wings, and they were invented in Buffalo, New York, in 1964, and they can't fly, as they're dinner.
Things with wings that can't fly.Theater stage: A trap: a theater stage has 'wings' on either side, the offstage areas where actors wait, and those certainly don't fly.
Things with wings that can't fly.Eagle: Eagles soar on thermals, and the bald eagle's wingspan can reach over two meters.
Things with wings that can't fly.Bat: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly, and their wings are really modified hands with skin stretched between the fingers.
Things with wings that can't fly.Bee: Bees flap their wings about 230 times per second, which makes their buzz.
Things with wings that can't fly.Airplane: Airplane wings generate lift because of their curved shape, and a jumbo jet's wings can span about 60 meters.
Things with wings that can't fly.Butterfly: Butterflies' wings are covered in tiny scales that make their colors, and the scales rub off like dust.
Things with wings that can't fly.Hummingbird: Hummingbirds can hover and even fly backward, and their wings beat around 50 times a second or more.
Things with wings that can't fly.Owl: Owls fly in near silence thanks to fringed wing feathers that muffle air turbulence.
Things with wings that can't fly.Seagull: Seagulls glide on ocean breezes, and many are strong fliers that follow ships for scraps.
Things with wings that can't fly.Dragonfly: Dragonflies can fly in any direction, including backward, and they're among the fastest insects, hitting over 50 km/h.
Things with wings that can't fly.Pigeon: Pigeons are strong fliers that can find their way home from hundreds of kilometers away, and they were used to carry messages in wartime.
Things with wings that can't fly.Glider: A glider has no engine but flies well, and the Wright brothers learned much from gliders before building their powered plane.
Things with wings that can't fly.Duck: Ducks are strong fliers, and some species migrate thousands of kilometers each year.
Things with wings that can't fly.Moth: A moth's wings are covered with scales like a butterfly's, and some moths navigate by the moon.
Things with wings that can't fly.Puffin: Puffins fly with rapid wingbeats, up to about 400 per minute, and they use their wings to swim underwater as well.

Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Flight: A cape isn't required. Superman, Thor and Iron Man all fly, while some characters like Batman rely on gliding or gadgets.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Super strength: Nearly every hero has it, though comics tend to vary the degree. The Hulk's strength reportedly grows with his anger.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.X-ray vision: Superman's signature power in comics since 1938. Real X-rays can't pass through lead, which is the hero's famous weak point.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Saving the world: The classic superhero goal. Marvel and DC stories repeatedly feature entire planets at risk, an impressive line for any résumé.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Teamwork: Even lone heroes need allies. Groups like the Avengers and Justice League show collaboration is a power in itself.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Invisibility: A power held by heroes like the Invisible Woman. Real-world cloaking research bends light around objects, but is far from working yet.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Crime fighting: The core job description. Detective Comics, the series that gave DC its name, introduced Batman in 1939.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Super speed: The Flash's trademark. Wally West, Barry Allen and others can in comic lore move faster than light.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Rescuing kittens: A classic hero cliché that shows kindness. Firefighters really do rescue cats, though 'cat stuck in a tree' calls are less common than jokes suggest.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Night patrols: Batman's specialty, as darkness suits his stealth. Plenty of crime-fighting stories happen after dark.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.World domination: A villain's dream, not a hero's skill. Supervillains from Doctor Doom to Lex Luthor have aimed for it.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Evil laugh: A villain trademark. The cackle is a cliché so established that it has a name, the 'Evil Laugh', in drama.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Bank robbery: Heroes stop robberies and never commit them. This villain staple is as old as the genre itself.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Doomsday device: A classic villain gadget. Its name also refers to a Superman villain, Doomsday, who famously killed the hero in 1992.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Hiring henchmen: Villains need underlings for dirty work, while heroes work alone or in teams. Henchmen are a classic spoof subject.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Ransom notes: Kidnappers' tools, not heroes'. The cut-out-letters style is a movie convention more than a real habit.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Stealing gold: Think Goldfinger in the James Bond novels, who schemed to irradiate Fort Knox's gold supply, not steal it.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Villainy: That's the whole job description of the other side. A hero's résumé would never mention it.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Lair building: Villains often have hidden volcano bases. Heroes tend to have mansions, caves or satellites, which arguably count as lairs too.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Treason: A betrayal of one's country, which is very much not heroic. Historically, it has been among the gravest crimes.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Mind control ray: A staple of villains' plots, since taking over minds is the ultimate evil shortcut. Heroes tend to protect free will.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Robbing museums: The kind of crime superheroes foil. In fiction, rogues like Catwoman have often stolen jewels and art.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Freeze ray heists: Think Mr. Freeze from Batman, who uses a freeze gun for crimes. It's a villainous skill, not a heroic one.
Things a superhero would put on a résumé.Moon laser plans: A very Bond-villain idea. The 1979 film Moonraker had a space station plot, so this is classic villain territory.

Things a hairdresser uses.Scissors: Professional hair shears often have an offset handle and can cost hundreds of dollars.
Things a hairdresser uses.Comb: Combs shaped from bone and wood have been found in graves over 5,000 years old.
Things a hairdresser uses.Hair dryer: Handheld electric dryers appeared around the 1920s, and early models were heavy and could get dangerously hot.
Things a hairdresser uses.Curling iron: In the 1870s, French hairdresser Marcel Grateau used heated tongs to create the Marcel wave, a huge fashion hit.
Things a hairdresser uses.Clippers: Guard numbers set the length, and a number 1 guard leaves about 3 millimeters of hair.
Things a hairdresser uses.Hair dye: People have colored hair for thousands of years, including with henna in ancient Egypt.
Things a hairdresser uses.Straightener: Flat irons heat ceramic plates to well over 150 degrees Celsius, which can damage hair if overused.
Things a hairdresser uses.Rollers: Heat styling works because hair's hydrogen bonds break and then re-form into a new shape as it cools.
Things a hairdresser uses.Salon cape: It keeps clippings off clothes, and some versions are waterproof for color work.
Things a hairdresser uses.Razor: Disposable blades arrived after King Camp Gillette's safety razor of the early 1900s, ending the barber's monopoly on a smooth shave.
Things a hairdresser uses.Hairbrush: Brushing 100 strokes a day is an old myth; too much brushing can actually break hair.
Things a hairdresser uses.Hairspray: Aerosol hairspray boomed in the 1950s, helped by teased and lacquered styles.
Things a hairdresser uses.Pinking shears: Their zigzag edge stops fabric from fraying, which makes them a seamstress's tool, not a hairdresser's.
Things a hairdresser uses.Pruning shears: Gardeners use them to snip living stems, and a hairdresser would never want such a hefty cutter.
Things a hairdresser uses.Trowel: A small hand shovel for gardens, or a pointed blade for spreading mortar; neither styles hair.
Things a hairdresser uses.Whisk: A balloon whisk beats air into eggs and cream, which is no help with hair.
Things a hairdresser uses.Hedge trimmer: Its reciprocating blades work like giant clippers, but they belong to garden work.
Things a hairdresser uses.Anvil: A blacksmith's block; a bone in your ear is also called the anvil.
Things a hairdresser uses.Ladle: The word comes from the Old English for loading, which is just what a ladle does with soup.
Things a hairdresser uses.Stethoscope: René Laennec invented it in 1816 by rolling up a sheet of paper to hear a patient's heart.
Things a hairdresser uses.Power drill: Black and Decker's pistol-grip drill of 1917 became the model for modern power drills.
Things a hairdresser uses.Sickle: A curved hand blade that has harvested cereal crops since the Stone Age.
Things a hairdresser uses.Lawn mower: Edwin Budding invented it in 1830 in England, adapting a machine used for trimming cloth.
Things a hairdresser uses.Scythe: A long curved blade for mowing, and also the tool carried by the Grim Reaper in art.

Things a DJ uses.Turntables: The Technics SL-1200, launched in 1972, became the DJ standard thanks to its steady direct-drive motor and pitch control.
Things a DJ uses.Headphones: DJs cue the next track in one ear to line up its beat before it reaches the crowd.
Things a DJ uses.Mixer: Channel faders and EQ knobs let a DJ cut one track's bass as another fades in, which is the core of smooth blending.
Things a DJ uses.Vinyl records: A 12-inch single spins at 45 rpm and an LP at 33 and a third, and DJs nudge the pitch to match tempos.
Things a DJ uses.Speakers: A club system can easily be loud enough to harm hearing; long exposure above about 85 decibels is where risk starts.
Things a DJ uses.Microphone: In early hip hop, DJs took the mic to hype the crowd before a separate MC role grew up to rap over the beats.
Things a DJ uses.Crossfader: A slider that blends between two decks; scratch DJs tune it to snap open instantly for rapid cuts.
Things a DJ uses.DJ controller: It packs decks and a mixer into one box, driving software like Serato or Rekordbox on a laptop.
Things a DJ uses.Laptop: Many DJs play from laptop software, where a sync feature can match two tracks' tempos automatically.
Things a DJ uses.Amplifier: It boosts a weak signal into thousands of watts for the speakers; DJs often plug into the venue's own rack.
Things a DJ uses.Conductor's baton: Jean-Baptiste Lully reportedly died in 1687 after stabbing his foot with the heavy staff he used to beat time.
Things a DJ uses.Easel: A painter's stand, from Dutch ezel, meaning donkey, because it carries the load.
Things a DJ uses.Stethoscope: René Laennec invented it in 1816, rolling up paper to avoid pressing his ear to a patient's chest.
Things a DJ uses.Sheet music stand: Classical players read from them; DJs follow waveforms on a screen instead of notation.
Things a DJ uses.Tuning fork: Trumpeter John Shore invented it in 1711; it rings at one pure pitch, such as the A at 440 hertz.
Things a DJ uses.Metronome: Patented by Johann Maelzel in 1815; DJs rely on BPM readouts instead of a ticking clock.
Things a DJ uses.Kiln: A potter's oven, hot enough to turn clay into ceramic at around 1,000 degrees Celsius or more.
Things a DJ uses.Loom: The Jacquard loom of 1804 used punched cards, an idea later borrowed by early computers.
Things a DJ uses.Trowel: Bricklayers spread mortar with it, and archaeologists use a small pointed one for careful digging.
Things a DJ uses.Gavel: A small mallet for calling order or sealing an auction sale; a DJ ends a set another way.
Things a DJ uses.Pitchfork: A farm tool for hay, and also the name of a famous music website, which makes it a tempting trap.
Things a DJ uses.Harp: A concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals, so it's an orchestra instrument, not DJ gear.
Things a DJ uses.Pipe organ: Called the king of instruments, the largest have tens of thousands of pipes, far beyond any DJ rig.
Things a DJ uses.Bagpipes: Air stored in the bag keeps the sound continuous, so pipers can play without pausing to breathe.

Things farmers do to crops.Sow: It means scattering or planting seeds, and farmers once threw seed by hand in broad arcs, a skill called broadcasting.
Things farmers do to crops.Harvest: Harvest festivals go back thousands of years, and the word comes from an Old English word for autumn.
Things farmers do to crops.Irrigate: Around 20 percent of the world's farmland is irrigated, yet it produces roughly 40 percent of the food.
Things farmers do to crops.Fertilize: The Haber-Bosch process, which captures nitrogen from the air, allows fertilizer that helps feed about half the world.
Things farmers do to crops.Weed: A weed is just a plant growing where it isn't wanted, and some, like dandelions, are edible.
Things farmers do to crops.Thresh: Threshing separates grain from stalks, once done by beating with a flail or trampling with oxen.
Things farmers do to crops.Prune: Cutting back branches helps fruit trees produce more and better fruit, and the practice goes back to ancient Greece and Rome.
Things farmers do to crops.Reap: Reaping with a sickle or scythe was the main method for centuries, until McCormick's mechanical reaper arrived in the 1830s.
Things farmers do to crops.Spray: Spraying crops with pesticides or fungicides protects them, and drones are now used in many fields for this.
Things farmers do to crops.Plant: Planting depth matters; many seeds need to be sown only about twice as deep as they are wide.
Things farmers do to crops.Shear: You shear sheep, not crops, and a good shearer can remove a fleece in about a minute, in one piece.
Things farmers do to crops.Milk: Milking is for animals, and a dairy cow produces around 25 liters of milk a day.
Things farmers do to crops.Brand: Branding is for cattle, to show ownership, and it is not something done to wheat or beans.
Things farmers do to crops.Herd: You herd livestock like cattle or sheep, and crops are rooted, so they can't be herded.
Things farmers do to crops.Groom: Grooming applies to horses and other animals, not crops, though some farmers prune hedges and lawn rows.
Things farmers do to crops.Saddle: Saddling a horse is a job for riders, not for plants.
Things farmers do to crops.Muck out: It means cleaning stables or barns of manure, which can then become fertilizer for the crops.
Things farmers do to crops.Vaccinate: Livestock get vaccinations, but crops depend on resistant varieties and sprays, not shots.
Things farmers do to crops.Lasso: A lasso, from Spanish "lazo", is a cowboy's rope for catching cattle and wild horses, not for fields.
Things farmers do to crops.Shoe: Farriers fit horseshoes, not crops, and nails go through the hoof's tough outer wall, which does not hurt the horse.
Things farmers do to crops.Hatch: Eggs hatch, and a chicken egg takes about 21 days, so it's a poultry task rather than a crop one.
Things farmers do to crops.Neuter: Neutering applies to animals such as pets and livestock, not to plants.
Things farmers do to crops.Bridle: A horse's bridle holds the bit and reins, and the word is of Old English origin; it isn't a crop job.
Things farmers do to crops.Pet: Farm animals can be pets, but crops don't need cuddles, though some say talking to plants helps.

Things printed on a store receipt.Date: Receipts print the date so you can prove when you bought something, which matters for returns and warranties.
Things printed on a store receipt.Total: The total is the amount you paid, and the point of the whole slip. It's usually printed in the boldest type.
Things printed on a store receipt.Tax: Tax is usually listed separately, so you can see how much of your payment goes to the government.
Things printed on a store receipt.Store name: The store name and address tell you where to take a return, and are usually printed at the top.
Things printed on a store receipt.Item prices: Each item's price is listed in a column, so you can check that the till charged you correctly for everything.
Things printed on a store receipt.Change given: Change given shows what was handed back after a cash payment, a useful check against till mistakes.
Things printed on a store receipt.Payment method: Receipts note if you paid by cash or card, often showing only the last four digits of the card number for safety.
Things printed on a store receipt.Receipt number: The receipt number lets the store look up the exact sale for returns, audits or warranty claims.
Things printed on a store receipt.Time: The time shows when the sale happened, useful to staff checking shift logs or security footage.
Things printed on a store receipt.Barcode: Many receipts print a barcode or QR code so the store can find the transaction fast for a return, or send you a survey.
Things printed on a store receipt.Customer's age: A shop doesn't record your age at the till, and it's private. Age checks happen at the counter, not on paper.
Things printed on a store receipt.Blood type: Blood type is a medical detail that never appears on a till slip, however personal the purchase.
Things printed on a store receipt.Weather: Weather isn't recorded on receipts, though the date and time pin down the day you bought something.
Things printed on a store receipt.Shoe size: Shoe size appears on a shoebox label or the price tag, not on the receipt, unless the item description includes it.
Things printed on a store receipt.Horoscope: A horoscope appears in newspapers and fortune cookies. A receipt only knows what you bought.
Things printed on a store receipt.Star rating: Star ratings appear in surveys and apps, though many receipts invite you to rate the store online.
Things printed on a store receipt.Recipe: A recipe belongs in a cookbook, not on a receipt, though the word 'receipt' once meant a recipe.
Things printed on a store receipt.Song lyrics: Song lyrics belong on album sleeves and screens, not on a till slip, which has little room anyway.
Things printed on a store receipt.Poem: A poem on a receipt would be a surprise, but receipt printers mostly list items and totals.
Things printed on a store receipt.Bedtime: A shop doesn't know your bedtime. The only time on the receipt is when you paid, which might be late at night.
Things printed on a store receipt.Menu: A menu lists what a restaurant offers, not what you bought. The receipt shows only what you ordered.
Things printed on a store receipt.Map: A map helps you find places, while a receipt only records a shop you've already visited. It has no use for directions.
Things printed on a store receipt.Lottery winner: Lottery winners are announced on draws, but Taiwan really does run a receipt lottery where the numbers on receipts can win prizes.
Things printed on a store receipt.Pet's name: A till slip has no field for your pet's name, however well the pet shop knows your dog or cat.

Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Butler: Butler comes from Old French for 'bottle-bearer', since early butlers looked after the wine cellar.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Footman: Footmen were named for running on foot beside carriages, and were often hired for their height and looks.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Valet: A valet looked after a gentleman's clothes and grooming, often travelling with him on visits.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Housemaid: Housemaids rose early to light fires and clean rooms before the family woke, and wore uniform.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Scullery maid: The scullery maid was the lowest-ranked servant, who washed pots and pans and did the hardest, dirtiest work.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Cook: Cooks were among the best paid servants and were called 'Mrs' by courtesy, whether or not they were married.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Governess: A governess taught children at home, a respectable job for educated women with few other options.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Coachman: A coachman drove the family carriage and cared for the horses, and ranked high among outdoor staff.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Gardener: Gardeners tended the grounds, and large estates had head gardeners who supervised teams and managed glasshouses.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Housekeeper: The housekeeper managed female staff and household supplies, and was called 'Mrs' regardless of marital status.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Lady's maid: A lady's maid dressed her mistress, styled her hair and mended clothes, and was among the most trusted servants.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Groom: A groom cared for horses and stables. The word also means a bridegroom, but the stable job is older.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Barista: A barista serves espresso. Coffee was drunk in Victorian times, but the job as we know it came in the late 20th century.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Programmer: A programmer writes software, a job that only exists since computers in the mid-20th century.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Influencer: Influencer is a modern job from social media, over a century too late for Victorian households.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Flight attendant: Flight attendants didn't exist until passenger air travel did, in the 1930s, so no Victorian had one.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Astronaut: Astronaut is a space-age job, born in the 1960s, long after the Victorian era had come to an end.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.DJ: A DJ plays recorded music and is a 20th-century job, since recordings and radio came later.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Personal trainer: Personal trainer is a modern fitness job, and an obvious anachronism for a Victorian estate.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Life coach: Life coach is a late 20th century job, and not a role that a Victorian servant would hold.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Data analyst: Data analyst is a computer-age job, so a Victorian household would never have employed one.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Web designer: A web designer needs the internet, which only reached the public in the 1990s, a century later.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Podcaster: Podcaster is a 21st-century job, much too late for Queen Victoria's household and all of her staff.
Jobs in a grand Victorian household.Software tester: Software tester is a modern job, so it has no place among the servants of a Victorian household.

Founded a famous tech company.Bill Gates: Gates co-founded Microsoft in 1975 with Paul Allen after dropping out of Harvard. He became a billionaire in his early thirties.
Founded a famous tech company.Steve Jobs: Jobs co-founded Apple in 1976, was pushed out in 1985, and returned in 1997. In between, he started NeXT and bought what became Pixar.
Founded a famous tech company.Mark Zuckerberg: Zuckerberg launched Facebook from his Harvard dorm in 2004. It reached a billion users by 2012, when he was still in his twenties.
Founded a famous tech company.Larry Page: Page co-founded Google in 1998 with Sergey Brin. The company's PageRank algorithm, named partly for him, ranked pages by the links pointing to them.
Founded a famous tech company.Sergey Brin: Brin co-founded Google with Larry Page while both were Stanford PhD students. Their first server was housed in a case made of Lego bricks.
Founded a famous tech company.Jeff Bezos: Bezos started Amazon in 1994 from his garage, first selling books online. He chose the name Amazon for the river's size, and early on it ranked alphabetically near the top.
Founded a famous tech company.Elon Musk: Musk co-founded X.com, which became PayPal, and later started SpaceX in 2002. He also joined Tesla early on and became its chief executive.
Founded a famous tech company.Jack Dorsey: Dorsey co-founded Twitter in 2006 and later started the payments company Square. The first tweet on the service was his, in March 2006.
Founded a famous tech company.Paul Allen: Allen co-founded Microsoft with Bill Gates in 1975. After leaving, he owned sports teams and funded a project to find shipwrecks, including a famous battleship.
Founded a famous tech company.Steve Wozniak: "Woz" designed the Apple I and Apple II by hand, and he's celebrated as the engineering mind behind Apple's early success.
Founded a famous tech company.Michael Dell: Dell began selling PC upgrades from his University of Texas dorm room in 1984 and founded Dell Computer. He became a billionaire before he was 40.
Founded a famous tech company.Larry Ellison: Ellison co-founded Oracle in 1977. The firm's name came from a CIA database project code-named Oracle, on which he had worked.
Founded a famous tech company.Jensen Huang: Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, reportedly in a Denny's diner. Its graphics chips, first for gamers, became the engines of the AI boom.
Founded a famous tech company.Tim Cook: Cook became Apple's CEO in 2011 when Steve Jobs stepped down. He is known for supply-chain expertise, not for founding the company.
Founded a famous tech company.Satya Nadella: Nadella became Microsoft's CEO in 2014, only its third. He joined the company in 1992, long after it was founded.
Founded a famous tech company.Sundar Pichai: Pichai became Google's CEO in 2015, and Alphabet's in 2019. He joined in 2004 and helped launch Chrome, rather than founding the company.
Founded a famous tech company.Sheryl Sandberg: Sandberg served as Facebook's chief operating officer from 2008. Her book Lean In made her famous, but she wasn't a founder.
Founded a famous tech company.Warren Buffett: Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway into a giant and is famous as an investor, not a tech founder. He long avoided tech stocks, then bought Apple.
Founded a famous tech company.Ada Lovelace: Lovelace wrote what's often called the first computer program in the 1840s, for Charles Babbage's design. It was long before any tech company existed.
Founded a famous tech company.Alan Turing: Turing laid the theoretical basis of computing and helped crack Enigma in World War II. He died in 1954, decades before today's tech companies were founded.
Founded a famous tech company.Andy Jassy: Jassy led Amazon Web Services and then took over from Jeff Bezos as Amazon's CEO in 2021. He's a leader of the company, not its founder.
Founded a famous tech company.Susan Wojcicki: Wojcicki rented her garage to Google's founders in 1998 and became employee number 16. She later ran YouTube, but she didn't found Google.
Founded a famous tech company.Steve Ballmer: Ballmer joined Microsoft in 1980 and became its CEO in 2000. He's remembered for a famous sweaty "Developers!" dance, not for founding it.
Founded a famous tech company.Lisa Su: Su became AMD's CEO in 2014 and helped pull the chipmaker back from the brink. She leads the company, but didn't found it.

Display technologies.LCD: Liquid crystal displays do not emit light themselves. They block or pass a backlight, which is why they need one.
Display technologies.LED: In TVs this usually means an LCD lit by LEDs rather than a self-glowing screen; the LED is just the backlight.
Display technologies.OLED: Each pixel makes its own light, so a black pixel is truly off. That gives the deep blacks OLED is famous for.
Display technologies.Plasma: Plasma screens lit tiny cells of gas into glowing, and were popular for big TVs in the 2000s before LCDs overtook them.
Display technologies.CRT: Cathode ray tubes fire an electron beam at a phosphor screen; they were the standard TV for over half a century.
Display technologies.E-ink: Used in e-readers, it only draws power when the page changes, so it can hold an image with the power off.
Display technologies.QLED: Samsung's name for an LCD that uses quantum dots to improve color; despite the name, it isn't an OLED.
Display technologies.AMOLED: An active-matrix OLED, common in phones and watches, uses a thin-film transistor layer to switch each pixel.
Display technologies.Mini-LED: Mini-LED backlights use thousands of tiny LEDs for finer dimming control on LCDs.
Display technologies.MicroLED: A tech where each pixel is a microscopic LED; it promises OLED-like contrast without burn-in but is very costly.
Display technologies.HDMI: This is a cable and connector standard, not a screen technology; it carries digital video and audio between devices.
Display technologies.USB: A connector standard for data and power. It can carry video too (USB-C), but it isn't a screen technology.
Display technologies.DVI: A digital video connector from 1999, common on PC monitors; it's a port, not a display type.
Display technologies.VGA: A 1987 IBM standard for graphics resolution and a blue 15-pin analog plug; it describes a signal, not panel technology.
Display technologies.SSD: A solid-state drive stores data in flash memory with no moving parts; it has nothing to do with screens.
Display technologies.RAM: Random access memory is the fast working memory of a computer, not a display.
Display technologies.CPU: The central processing unit is the computer's main processor, not a display technology.
Display technologies.Wi-Fi: A wireless networking standard; the name was invented by a branding firm and doesn't stand for anything technical.
Display technologies.Bluetooth: Named after a Danish Viking king, Harald Bluetooth, it's a short-range wireless link, not a screen.
Display technologies.NFC: Near-field communication enables tap-to-pay; it works over just a few centimeters, and it has no display role.
Display technologies.HDD: The hard disk drive stores data on spinning magnetic platters, not display pixels.
Display technologies.BIOS: The firmware that starts a PC before the operating system loads; it's software, not a display tech.
Display technologies.DisplayPort: A video connector standard from VESA, introduced in 2006, so it carries a picture but isn't a screen technology.
Display technologies.Ethernet: Invented at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, it is a wired networking standard, not a display.

Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Magic beans: Jack gets them by trading the family cow; the phrase "magic beans" now means a dubious, too-good-to-be-true bargain.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Beanstalk: The tale appeared in English print in 1734 and was popularized by Joseph Jacobs in 1890; the giant plant grows overnight.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Giant: In Benjamin Tabart's 1807 retelling, the giant had murdered Jack's father, which gave Jack's thefts a moral excuse.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Cow: Often named Milky-White, the cow is sold for beans, starting the adventure; her trade sets off every other event.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Golden harp: When Jack steals it, the harp cries out "Master! Master!", which wakes the sleeping giant in many versions.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Golden hen: It lays golden eggs on command, and some tellings make it a goose; Aesop's separate fable also has a golden-egg goose.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Fee-fi-fo-fum: The giant's chant ends with smelling the blood of an Englishman; Shakespeare's King Lear has Edgar chant a close cousin.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Axe: Jack grabs an axe and chops down the beanstalk as the giant climbs after him, sending the giant crashing to his death.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Bag of gold: The first thing Jack steals from the castle is a bag of gold coins, which keeps him and his mother going for a while.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Giant's wife: She often hides Jack in the oven or a cupboard and sometimes helps him, making her more kindly than her husband.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Castle: Folklorists classify this tale as ATU 328, "The Treasures of the Giant", a type found across many European cultures.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Jack's mother: Her fury at the worthless beans leads her to hurl them out the window, which is why the stalk sprouts by morning.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Glass slipper: That's Cinderella's. Perrault's 1697 version made her slipper glass, though earlier tellings had no such shoe.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Poisoned apple: That's Snow White's. In the Grimms' version, the queen disguises herself as a peddler to deliver it.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Spinning wheel: That's Sleeping Beauty's. Pricking a finger on the spindle sends her into a hundred-year sleep in the Grimms' version.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Red hood: Little Red Riding Hood wears it; Charles Perrault made the hood red in his 1697 version.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Breadcrumbs: Hansel and Gretel use these to mark their trail, and birds eat them. Computers borrowed the idea for navigation links.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Pumpkin: Cinderella's fairy godmother turns one into a coach; the pumpkin comes from Perrault's version, not the Grimms'.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Seven dwarfs: Snow White's helpers had no names in the Grimms' tale; Disney's 1937 film invented Doc, Grumpy, Sleepy and the rest.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Pea: Hans Christian Andersen's "The Princess and the Pea" (1835) has a real princess feeling one pea under twenty mattresses.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Frog: In the Grimms' Frog Prince, the princess hurls the frog against a wall rather than kissing him; the kiss came later.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Magic mirror: Snow White's queen has it; in Disney it's "Magic mirror on the wall", but the Grimms wrote "looking-glass".
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Tower: Rapunzel's tower, with no door and a window only at the top, belongs to a Grimm tale of 1812.
Things in Jack and the Beanstalk.Porridge: Goldilocks eats the bears' porridge. In Robert Southey's 1837 original, the intruder was a rude old woman, not a girl.

Things that are usually black.Coal: Coal is made from ancient plant matter, and it is mostly carbon, which is why it burns.
Things that are usually black.Crow: Crows can recognise human faces and hold grudges, passing the knowledge to other crows.
Things that are usually black.Raven: Ravens are bigger than crows, with a wedge-shaped tail, and they are known for solving puzzles.
