Things that are usually black.Car tire: Tires are black because of carbon black added to the rubber, which strengthens it and protects it from UV light.
Things that are usually black.Tar: Tar is a dark sticky substance from coal, wood or oil, and the La Brea Tar Pits in LA trapped ice-age animals.
Things that are usually black.Charcoal: Charcoal is wood burned with little air, leaving black carbon, and it is used in barbecues and drawing.
Things that are usually black.Hockey puck: Pucks are frozen before games to reduce bounce, and they are made of vulcanised rubber.
Things that are usually black.Darth Vader: The Star Wars villain's voice was James Earl Jones, and the suit was an actor, David Prowse.
Things that are usually black.Asphalt: Asphalt roads are black because of bitumen, a thick oil product that binds the gravel together.
Things that are usually black.Blackberry: Blackberries are dark purple-black, and they're not true berries but aggregates of tiny drupelets.
Things that are usually black.Gorilla: Adult male gorillas get silver back hair, and the species is named for it, though most of their fur is black.
Things that are usually black.Snow: Snow is white, because ice crystals scatter light, so it's not a black thing.
Things that are usually black.Milk: Milk is white, which comes from its fat and protein particles.
Things that are usually black.Polar bear: Polar bears look white but have black skin underneath, and the fur itself is transparent.
Things that are usually black.Banana: Bananas are yellow, and brown spots on one mean it's ripe.
Things that are usually black.Fire truck: Fire trucks are usually red, so they stand out.
Things that are usually black.Sunflower: Sunflowers are yellow, though they turn to follow the sun when young.
Things that are usually black.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are orange, though some varieties are white, green or blue.
Things that are usually black.Lime: Limes are green, and they're named from the Persian "limu".
Things that are usually black.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink, and the colour comes from their diet, not from their genes.
Things that are usually black.Canary: Canaries are yellow, and the Canary Islands are the source of the bird's name.
Things that are usually black.Sky: The sky looks blue by day because air scatters blue light more, and at night it is dark, though not truly black.
Things that are usually black.Strawberry: Strawberries are red, with tiny seeds on the outside.
Things that are usually black.Cauliflower: Cauliflower is normally white, but it comes in purple, orange and green types as well.

Things full of holes.Sponge: A sponge's holes aren't just decoration; the animal's pores pull in water to filter food.
Things full of holes.Swiss cheese: Swiss researchers found that tiny hay particles in milk seed the holes in Swiss cheese, and cleaner milking means fewer holes.
Things full of holes.Colander: The word colander comes from the Latin 'colare', meaning to strain.
Things full of holes.Fishing net: Fishing nets are mostly holes by design, and the technology is many thousands of years old.
Things full of holes.Sieve: Sieves have been used since ancient Egypt, and labs use standardized mesh sizes to sort sand and soil.
Things full of holes.Wiffle ball: Wiffle balls were invented in 1953 in Connecticut, and the holes make them curve; the name comes from 'whiff', a strikeout.
Things full of holes.Lace: Lace is a fabric that is mostly holes, and early handmade lace was so laborious it was a European status symbol.
Things full of holes.Crumpet: A crumpet gets its holes from yeast bubbles bursting on the griddle, perfect for soaking up melted butter.
Things full of holes.Salt shaker: Salt shakers sometimes get a few grains of rice in them because the rice absorbs moisture and keeps salt flowing.
Things full of holes.Shower head: Hard-water minerals can clog a shower head's holes, and a vinegar soak usually clears them.
Things full of holes.Crocs: Crocs began in 2002 as a boating shoe, and the holes were meant to drain water and add ventilation.
Things full of holes.Pegboard: Julia Child famously outlined her pots on a pegboard in her kitchen, so each had its home.
Things full of holes.Cheese grater: Microplane graters began as woodworking rasps before cooks discovered they were excellent for zesting.
Things full of holes.Golf ball: A golf ball's dimples are dents, not holes, and they reduce drag so the ball flies farther.
Things full of holes.Balloon: A latex balloon has no holes, but helium slips through microscopic pores, which is why it sags overnight.
Things full of holes.Dinner plate: A dinner plate is solid, which is why it can hold soup and why you can't sieve with it.
Things full of holes.Mirror: A mirror is glass backed with a thin metal layer, a solid surface with no holes.
Things full of holes.Egg: A hen's eggshell has thousands of microscopic pores so the chick can breathe, but it has no real holes.
Things full of holes.Marble: A marble is solid glass, usually about 16 millimeters across.
Things full of holes.Window pane: A window pane is a solid sheet of glass, a perfect lack of holes.
Things full of holes.Apple: An apple floats because about a quarter of its volume is air in tiny spaces, but it has no holes.
Things full of holes.Spoon: A spoon is solid unless it is slotted, and the oldest ones were carved from wood, bone or shell.
Things full of holes.Bucket: A bucket's whole job is holding water, which is why the folk song 'There's a hole in my bucket' is a problem.
Things full of holes.Frying pan: A frying pan is solid, and its non-stick coating, PTFE, was discovered by accident in 1938.

Things with a shell.Turtle: A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton, fused to its ribs and spine, so it can't ever crawl out of it.
Things with a shell.Snail: A snail's shell grows in a spiral as the animal does, and most species coil clockwise.
Things with a shell.Egg: A hen's eggshell is mostly calcium carbonate and has thousands of tiny pores, which lets the chick breathe inside.
Things with a shell.Crab: A crab outgrows its shell by molting, and while the new one hardens it is soft, vulnerable and hides.
Things with a shell.Lobster: Lobsters turn red when cooked because heat breaks down proteins that mask the red pigment astaxanthin in their shells.
Things with a shell.Clam: Clams have two hinged shells, and by counting the growth rings on a shell, scientists can estimate the animal's age.
Things with a shell.Oyster: An oyster makes a pearl by coating an irritant in layers of nacre, though most pearls are made by cultured farming.
Things with a shell.Armadillo: The nine-banded armadillo almost always gives birth to identical quadruplets, and its shell is made of bony plates.
Things with a shell.Walnut: A walnut's hard shell is the seed's protective casing, and it is the inside kernel we eat.
Things with a shell.Peanut: A peanut's papery shell is really a pod, and the peanut is technically a legume, not a nut.
Things with a shell.Pistachio: A pistachio's shell splits open naturally when the seed ripens, and the nut is a seed of a relative of the cashew.
Things with a shell.Scallop: Scallops have up to about 200 tiny eyes along the edge of their shell, and they swim by clapping the shells together.
Things with a shell.Coconut: A coconut has a husk, a hard shell and a layer of white meat; the shell is often used as a bowl or charcoal.
Things with a shell.Slug: A slug is basically a snail without a shell, though many carry a tiny remnant inside the body.
Things with a shell.Octopus: Octopuses lack a shell, so their bodies are so flexible they can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak.
Things with a shell.Jellyfish: A jellyfish has no shell, brain or heart, and its body is about 95 percent water.
Things with a shell.Frog: Frogs have no shell, and their thin, permeable skin lets them absorb water and even breathe through it.
Things with a shell.Earthworm: Earthworms have no shell and no lungs, breathing through their skin, which must stay moist.
Things with a shell.Banana: A banana has a peel, not a shell, and it's a berry on a giant herb rather than a tree.
Things with a shell.Grape: A grape has a thin skin rather than a shell, and its waxy coating makes it look dusty.
Things with a shell.Salmon: Salmon are covered in scales, not a shell, and they return to the stream where they hatched, using smell to find it.
Things with a shell.Hedgehog: A hedgehog's protection is spines, not a shell, and each one is a hollow modified hair, with about 5,000 on one animal.
Things with a shell.Seal: Seals have thick blubber and fur, not a shell, and some can dive for over an hour on a single breath.
Things with a shell.Raisin: A raisin is a dried grape with no shell, and it takes roughly four pounds of grapes to make one pound of raisins.

Airports, not train stations.Heathrow: London's busiest airport sits west of the city, and a 2000s plan for a third runway sparked decades of political fights over noise and emissions.
Airports, not train stations.Changi: Singapore's airport features an indoor waterfall called the Rain Vortex, among the tallest indoor waterfalls in the world, inside the Jewel complex.
Airports, not train stations.Schiphol: Amsterdam's airport is partly below sea level, and its urinals famously feature a fly etched in the porcelain to improve aim and cut cleaning costs.
Airports, not train stations.O'Hare: Chicago's O'Hare is named after WWII hero Butch O'Hare, and it was once the world's busiest airport by takeoffs and landings.
Airports, not train stations.Gatwick: London's second-largest airport started as a racecourse in the 1890s, and later its single runway grew into the busiest in the world.
Airports, not train stations.Dulles: Washington's airport is named for John Foster Dulles, and its swooping roofed terminal was designed by Eero Saarinen, who also designed the Gateway Arch.
Airports, not train stations.JFK: New York's main international gateway began as Idlewild Airport and was renamed in 1963, a month after President Kennedy's assassination.
Airports, not train stations.LaGuardia: This New York airport is named for mayor Fiorello La Guardia, who pushed for a city airport after a 1930s flight left him stranded at the wrong airport.
Airports, not train stations.Charles de Gaulle: Paris's big airport (CDG) has its terminals arranged around a giant circle, and Terminal 1 looks like a concrete flying saucer from the 1970s.
Airports, not train stations.Narita: Tokyo's international gateway opened in 1978 after violent farmland protests, and it's far from the city, about an hour away by express train.
Airports, not train stations.Logan: Boston's airport is named for Edward Lawrence Logan, a general, and sits on reclaimed land in the harbor, so planes land close to the water.
Airports, not train stations.Orly: Paris's second airport is south of the city, and it was once the capital's biggest hub until Charles de Gaulle took over most international traffic.
Airports, not train stations.Stansted: London's third big airport has a sleek glass terminal by Norman Foster, and it's a hub for budget carriers, especially Ryanair.
Airports, not train stations.Wembley: A stadium in London, not an airport. The venue holds around 90,000 and is known for its giant arch, which is visible across north London.
Airports, not train stations.Paddington: A London railway terminal, not an airport. Its brick-and-iron shed by Brunel inspired the famous bear who arrived from Peru with a marmalade sandwich.
Airports, not train stations.Grand Central: A New York train terminal with a ceiling painted with constellations, and it has more platforms than any other station in the world, at 44.
Airports, not train stations.Penn Station: New York's busiest rail hub, mostly underground. The original grand 1910 building was demolished in the 1960s, sparking the preservation movement.
Airports, not train stations.Waterloo: London's busiest station is named after Napoleon's 1815 defeat, and it was once the site of the Eurostar terminal before King's Cross St Pancras.
Airports, not train stations.Euston: London terminus for trains to northwest England and Scotland, and its original Doric Arch was torn down in 1960s, a loss still lamented.
Airports, not train stations.Shinjuku: Tokyo's rail station is said to handle around three million passengers on an average day, making it the busiest station in the world.
Airports, not train stations.Union Station: Name shared by many big rail stations in North America, and Washington's has a vast Beaux-Arts hall; it's a trap since there's no airport here.
Airports, not train stations.Fenway: A Boston ballpark, not a transport hub. Opened in 1912, it's America's oldest Major League stadium and has the towering Green Monster wall.
Airports, not train stations.Alcatraz: A San Francisco Bay island that was a federal prison, not an airport. It held Al Capone and is also a rocky isle with a famous lighthouse.
Airports, not train stations.King's Cross: A London train terminal famed for Platform 9 and three-quarters in Harry Potter, but it's a train station, not an airport.

Kinds of road.Highway: Highway originally meant any main public road, and in the United States the Interstate system, begun in 1956, stretches about 75,000 kilometers.
Kinds of road.Motorway: Britain's first motorway, the Preston Bypass, opened in 1958, and motorways ban slow vehicles like bicycles and tractors.
Kinds of road.Freeway: A freeway has no tolls and no cross traffic; California's Arroyo Seco Parkway, opened in 1940 near Los Angeles, is often called the first in the West.
Kinds of road.Avenue: Avenue comes from French for approaching, and the term originally described a tree-lined approach to a grand house.
Kinds of road.Boulevard: Boulevard originally referred to the ramparts of a fortress, which Paris turned into broad promenades lined with trees.
Kinds of road.Lane: Lane is the narrowest country road, and in cities it also names a strip of a wider road marked for one line of traffic.
Kinds of road.Cul-de-sac: Cul-de-sac is French for bottom of the bag, and a street with a dead end that ends in a circle is its classic form.
Kinds of road.Alley: Alleys run behind buildings for deliveries and trash, and some, like the narrow ones in Venice, are real tourist routes.
Kinds of road.Expressway: Expressways are fast roads with limited access, and in many cities they replaced neighborhoods when they were built through them.
Kinds of road.Turnpike: The word comes from spiked barriers that turned aside traffic until a toll was paid, and the first turnpikes appeared in 17th-century England.
Kinds of road.Dual carriageway: A dual carriageway has a central strip separating opposite directions, which makes head-on collisions far less common than on two-way roads.
Kinds of road.Bypass: A bypass lets traffic skip a town center, and medical bypass surgery uses the same idea to route blood around a blocked artery.
Kinds of road.Toll road: The ancient Romans already charged road tolls, and electronic tolling now lets cars pass without stopping.
Kinds of road.Canal: Canals are for boats rather than cars, and the Grand Canal in China, over 1,700 kilometers long, is the longest in the world.
Kinds of road.Runway: Runways are numbered by compass heading, so one aimed roughly east is called 09, for 90 degrees.
Kinds of road.Railway: Railway tracks are usually spaced 1,435 millimeters apart, a width called standard gauge, used across much of the world.
Kinds of road.Sidewalk: A sidewalk is a path beside a road for people on foot, and it is a walkway rather than a road for vehicles.
Kinds of road.Taxiway: Taxiways link runways to terminals, and aircraft use them to taxi at modest speeds.
Kinds of road.Pier: A pier extends into water on pillars, and Brighton's famous Victorian one has featured amusements for over a century.
Kinds of road.Moat: A moat is a defensive ditch filled with water around a castle, and it was meant to keep attackers from reaching walls.
Kinds of road.Aqueduct: Roman aqueducts carried water by gravity over long distances, and some, like Segovia's, still stand after about 2,000 years.
Kinds of road.Ski slope: Ski slopes are graded by color and difficulty, and the steepest black runs may drop at a pitch over 40 degrees.
Kinds of road.Hiking trail: The Appalachian Trail runs about 3,500 kilometers from Georgia to Maine, but trails are for walkers, not true roads.
Kinds of road.River: Rivers can carry boats as natural highways, and the Nile historically served as ancient Egypt's main route, though it isn't a road.

Types of bus.Double-decker: London's red Routemaster double-decker entered service in 1956, and its open rear platform let passengers hop on and off.
Types of bus.Minibus: In many countries minibuses are the backbone of public transport, such as Kenya's matatus and South Africa's minibus taxis.
Types of bus.School bus: American school buses are yellow because a 1939 conference chose a shade, 'National School Bus Chrome', that is easy to spot.
Types of bus.Coach: The word coach comes from the Hungarian town of Kocs, where a famous type of carriage was made.
Types of bus.Trolleybus: A trolleybus draws power from two overhead wires, since it has rubber tires and so can't use the rails as the return path.
Types of bus.Shuttle bus: Shuttle comes from a weaving loom's tool that moves back and forth, which is what a shuttle bus does.
Types of bus.Tour bus: Open-top tour buses have been showing off cities since the 1950s, and 'hop-on hop-off' tickets let people hop on and off.
Types of bus.Party bus: Party buses are typically converted vehicles fitted with lights and a sound system, and are hired for celebrations.
Types of bus.Bendy bus: London phased out its bendy buses in 2011, since the accordion joint made them hard to maneuver in narrow streets.
Types of bus.Tram: Trams run on rails in city streets, which is why they're not buses.
Types of bus.Streetcar: Streetcars are the American name for trams, and they run on rails.
Types of bus.Monorail: A monorail runs on a single beam, and the Seattle one built for the 1962 World's Fair still operates.
Types of bus.Caboose: The caboose was the crew car at the end of freight trains, and it disappeared in the 1980s with electronic end-of-train devices.
Types of bus.Hearse: A hearse carries coffins to funerals, so it is a vehicle but not a bus.
Types of bus.Limousine: Limousines are named for the French region of Limousin, whose cloak-like hooded fashion inspired the covered driver's compartment.
Types of bus.Taxi: A taxi is hired by a single party, unlike a bus that serves many riders on a fixed route.
Types of bus.Camper van: A camper van is a vehicle with sleeping space, but it is private, not for public transport.
Types of bus.Pickup: A pickup is a truck with an open cargo bed, so it is not a bus.
Types of bus.Tuk-tuk: A tuk-tuk is a three-wheeled motorized taxi, and it can't hold the crowd of a bus.
Types of bus.Subway: A subway runs underground on tracks, so it is a train, not a bus.
Types of bus.Funicular: A funicular climbs steep slopes pulled by cables on rails, so it is not a bus.
Types of bus.Cable car: A cable car hangs from or is pulled by a cable, and San Francisco's famous ones grip a moving cable under the street.
Types of bus.Rickshaw: A rickshaw is pulled by a person or pedaled by a cyclist, so it is not a bus.
Types of bus.Minivan: A minivan looks like a mini-bus, but it's a small family car with room for about seven, not a bus.

Types of jewelry.Necklace: Necklaces are among the oldest jewelry, with shell beads found in Africa dating back about 75,000 years.
Types of jewelry.Bracelet: The word comes from Latin for 'arm'. Ancient Egyptians wore bracelets of gold, and some were buried alongside pharaohs.
Types of jewelry.Brooch: Brooches began as practical pins fastening cloaks. Queen Victoria's collection helped make them a fashion statement.
Types of jewelry.Anklet: Anklets have been worn since ancient times in Egypt and India. In India they often carry tiny bells that jingle as the wearer walks.
Types of jewelry.Pendant: A pendant hangs from a chain or cord. Some of the earliest were carved amulets worn for protection.
Types of jewelry.Earring: Earrings are documented in ancient Persia and Mesopotamia. Ötzi the Iceman, over 5,000 years old, had stretched earlobes for ornaments.
Types of jewelry.Tiara: A tiara is a jeweled crown-like band, usually worn by royalty at formal occasions. Ancient Persian kings wore a related headdress.
Types of jewelry.Locket: Lockets hold a tiny portrait or lock of hair. Victorians popularized them as mourning jewelry.
Types of jewelry.Cufflink: Cufflinks fasten shirt cuffs. They became fashionable after French-cuff shirts arrived in the 1800s.
Types of jewelry.Choker: A choker is a close-fitting necklace, and the velvet-ribbon version was a Victorian fashion that returned in the 1990s.
Types of jewelry.Bangle: A rigid, unclasped bracelet. The word comes from the Hindi 'bangri', and bangles are central to South Asian weddings.
Types of jewelry.Signet ring: Signet rings carry an engraved emblem, used for centuries to press a seal in hot wax and prove a letter was authentic.
Types of jewelry.Nose ring: Nose rings are documented in the Middle East by about 4,000 years ago, and remain a bridal tradition in India.
Types of jewelry.Cravat: Cravats are neckwear, not jewelry. The name comes from 'Croat', after Croatian soldiers whose scarves inspired the style.
Types of jewelry.Lanyard: A lanyard is a cord for carrying ID or keys. It is not decorative jewelry, though it hangs around the neck.
Types of jewelry.Suspenders: Suspenders, called braces in Britain, hold up trousers with straps over the shoulders. They are clothing hardware, not ornament.
Types of jewelry.Scarf: A scarf is a fabric accessory, not a jewel. Ancient Chinese soldiers wore silk scarves as marks of rank.
Types of jewelry.Bow tie: Bow ties started as a practical way to hold shirt collars closed. Formal ones are still hand-tied, but they count as neckwear, not jewelry.
Types of jewelry.Hairnet: A hairnet keeps hair out of food or machinery. It is a hygiene item, worn by kitchen staff, with no decorative value.
Types of jewelry.Corsage: A corsage is a small flower arrangement worn at the wrist or lapel. Fresh flowers, not metal or gems.
Types of jewelry.Monocle: The monocle is a single eyeglass lens held by the eye socket, and it is an optical aid, not jewelry despite its fancy reputation.
Types of jewelry.Sash: A sash is a band of cloth worn around the waist or over the shoulder, as for pageant winners.
Types of jewelry.Garter: A garter holds up stockings. It is underwear, although bridal garters are a wedding custom.
Types of jewelry.Headphones: Headphones are electronics, not jewelry. The first pair, from 1910, was made by hand for the US Navy.

Sleeve styles.Raglan: The seam runs diagonally from collar to underarm, with no shoulder seam, as on baseball jerseys; named after Lord Raglan.
Sleeve styles.Cap: A cap sleeve barely covers the shoulder, with just a small cap of fabric rather than a full sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Bell: The bell sleeve widens toward the wrist, a medieval look that fashion keeps reviving.
Sleeve styles.Puff: Princess Diana's 1981 wedding dress had enormous puff sleeves, which made the style a symbol of the decade.
Sleeve styles.Bishop: Gathered at the wrist and full above it, named after the flowing sleeves of a bishop's robes.
Sleeve styles.Dolman: Cut wide at the armhole and narrow at the wrist, from the Turkish dolama, a long robe.
Sleeve styles.Batwing: A very loose cousin of the dolman, shaped like wings when you raise your arms, and big in the 1980s.
Sleeve styles.Leg-of-mutton: Huge at the top and tight below the elbow, a Victorian 1890s balloon silhouette that looks like a sheep's leg.
Sleeve styles.Three-quarter: Ends midway between the elbow and the wrist, a length that suits work and warmth.
Sleeve styles.Lantern: Puffed at the lower end and gathered at the wrist, shaped a bit like a paper lantern.
Sleeve styles.Bootcut: A trap: bootcut describes jeans that fit over boots, and it is a leg, not a sleeve.
Sleeve styles.V-neck: A V-neck is a neckline, shaped like the letter V, not a sleeve style.
Sleeve styles.Crew neck: A crew neck is named for rowing crews' sweaters, and it describes the neckline, not the sleeves.
Sleeve styles.Halter: A halter has straps going around the neck, named after a horse halter, and it is a neckline.
Sleeve styles.Sweetheart: A sweetheart neckline is shaped like the top of a heart, so it is a neckline rather than a sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Cowl neck: Cowl comes from Latin cuculla, a monk's hood, and it describes a draped neckline, not a sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Peplum: A peplum is a ruffle at the waist, from the Greek peplos, so it's not a sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Pencil: A pencil skirt is a slim, narrow skirt, which makes it a skirt, not a sleeve style.
Sleeve styles.A-line: The A-line was introduced by Dior in 1955, and it describes a skirt or dress silhouette, not a sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Pleated: Pleats are folds in fabric, a texture of cloth rather than a kind of sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Turtleneck: A turtleneck is a high rolled collar, called a polo neck in Britain, so it is a neckline.
Sleeve styles.Empire waist: The empire waist sits just under the bust, popularized by Empress Josephine, and it is a waistline.
Sleeve styles.Drop waist: The drop waist is a low waistline typical of 1920s flapper dresses, so it is not a sleeve.
Sleeve styles.Boat neck: The boat neck is a neckline, called bateau in French, and it is not a sleeve.

Fictional languages.Klingon: Marc Okrand built it for Star Trek with object-verb-subject word order, and fans have translated Hamlet and even the Bible into it.
Fictional languages.Quenya: Tolkien's High-Elven tongue, partly modeled on Finnish. He said he invented his languages first and wrote stories to give them a world.
Fictional languages.Sindarin: Tolkien's everyday Elvish, inspired by Welsh. It's the language of the Doors of Durin inscription: "Speak, friend, and enter."
Fictional languages.Dothraki: Linguist David J. Peterson built it for Game of Thrones from only a few phrases in George R. R. Martin's novels, then grew it into a full language.
Fictional languages.Na'vi: Linguist Paul Frommer created it for Avatar, with its own grammar and sounds. Fans around the world now study and speak it online.
Fictional languages.Newspeak: Orwell's language in 1984 shrinks the vocabulary on purpose, so rebellious thoughts become impossible to even express.
Fictional languages.Parseltongue: The snake tongue of Harry Potter. Harry first speaks it by accident at the zoo, and it's seen as a mark of Slytherin and Voldemort.
Fictional languages.Huttese: The language of Jabba and the Hutts. Sound designer Ben Burtt built it from real languages, notably the Andean tongue Quechua.
Fictional languages.Simlish: The gibberish of The Sims was designed so players wouldn't be distracted by real dialogue. Real pop stars have recorded songs in it.
Fictional languages.High Valyrian: Another David J. Peterson creation for Game of Thrones. It has complex grammar and was built to feel like an ancient, dying tongue.
Fictional languages.Nadsat: Anthony Burgess invented this teenage slang for A Clockwork Orange, mostly Russian words bent into English, such as "droog" for friend.
Fictional languages.Minionese: The Minions' babble mixes English, Spanish, Italian, French and more, with real words tucked in, so listeners can half-follow it.
Fictional languages.Esperanto: Esperanto is constructed but real: L. L. Zamenhof published it in 1887 for actual use, and some people have grown up speaking it natively.
Fictional languages.Basque: A real language isolate, unrelated to any other living language. It's spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France.
Fictional languages.Tagalog: The base of Filipino, the national language of the Philippines. It's real, and full of Spanish loanwords like "mesa" for table.
Fictional languages.Swahili: A real Bantu language spoken across East Africa. "Hakuna matata" in The Lion King is genuine Swahili for "no worries."
Fictional languages.Latin: No longer anyone's native tongue, but real, and still the official language of Vatican City. Its vocabulary is all over English.
Fictional languages.Tok Pisin: A real English-based creole and an official language of Papua New Guinea. "Pisin" is simply how the word "pidgin" sounds.
Fictional languages.Yiddish: Real: a blend of German, Hebrew and Slavic languages. English borrowed "chutzpah" and "klutz" from it.
Fictional languages.Faroese: A real language of the Faroe Islands, spoken by around 50,000 people and still close to Old Norse.
Fictional languages.Maori: The real Indigenous language of New Zealand, made an official language in 1987. Words like "kiwi" and "haka" are well known worldwide.
Fictional languages.Cherokee: A real language with a syllabary invented by Sequoyah in the 1820s. Within a few years, much of the Cherokee Nation could read.
Fictional languages.Sanskrit: A real ancient language of India, still used in religious texts. It's a distant cousin of Latin and Greek.
Fictional languages.Afrikaans: A real language that grew out of Dutch in South Africa. It's among the youngest of the Germanic languages.

Objects from classic fairy tales.Glass slipper: Cinderella's footwear. The glass may come from a mistranslation, as some say, of old French "vair" (fur) as "verre" (glass).
Objects from classic fairy tales.Poisoned apple: Snow White takes a bite of the apple, and falls into a deathlike sleep. It works as a poison disguised as a treat.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Spinning wheel: A spindle prick sends Sleeping Beauty into her 100-year sleep, so the spinning wheel is the trap that starts it.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Magic beans: Jack trades the family cow for them, and they grow into a giant beanstalk overnight.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Gingerbread house: The witch's candy cottage in Hansel and Gretel, built from bread, cake and sugar to lure hungry children.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Pumpkin coach: Cinderella's pumpkin carriage turns back at midnight, when the fairy godmother's magic ends.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Magic mirror: The Snow White queen's mirror tells her who is fairest in the land, and cannot lie.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Breadcrumbs: Hansel drops them to find the way home, but birds eat the trail, so the children are lost.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Glass coffin: Snow White's resting place, where she seems dead before a prince's servants jolt her awake.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Golden harp: In Jack and the Beanstalk, the giant's magical golden harp plays and sings by itself, and Jack steals it.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Ruby slippers: Trap: in Baum's book, Dorothy's shoes were silver. The film made them ruby to show off Technicolor.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Golden Snitch: Harry Potter's tiny winged ball, worth 150 points in Quidditch. It belongs to J. K. Rowling's world.
Objects from classic fairy tales.One Ring: Tolkien's ring of power, forged by Sauron to rule Middle-earth. It belongs to fantasy fiction, not classic fairy tales.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Crystal skull: An object from an Indiana Jones film, not from a classic fairy tale.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Sword in the stone: King Arthur's tale is an Arthurian legend, not a classic fairy tale like Cinderella.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Invisibility cloak: Harry Potter's cloak that makes you invisible is a modern fantasy item, not from an old fairy tale.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Time-Turner: Hermione's device for traveling back a few hours is from Harry Potter, not a classic fairy tale.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Holy Grail: The Grail is a Christian legend tied to the Last Supper and Arthur's knights, not a classic fairy tale.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Philosopher's Stone: An alchemy legend about a stone said to turn metals into gold. It's not a classic fairy-tale object.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Golden Fleece: Jason and the Argonauts sought it in Greek myth: a ram's golden wool. A myth, not a fairy tale.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Lightsaber: Star Wars's glowing laser-like blade is a modern science-fiction invention, not a classic fairy-tale object.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Infinity Gauntlet: Marvel's glove that holds six powerful stones. It belongs to comics and film, not classic fairy tales.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Pandora's box: In Greek myth, it was a jar, not a box, and a mistranslation by Erasmus created the box. A myth, not a fairy tale.
Objects from classic fairy tales.Elder Wand: The Elder Wand is the most powerful in Harry Potter, a modern fantasy item and not from classic tales.

Penguin species.Emperor: The tallest penguin at about 1.1 meters; males balance the egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter.
Penguin species.King: The second-largest; it carries its single egg on its feet without a nest, and chicks take over a year to fledge.
Penguin species.Adelie: A hardy Antarctic penguin whose males offer pebbles to attract mates and build nests.
Penguin species.Gentoo: The fastest-swimming penguin, reaching about 36 km/h underwater.
Penguin species.Chinstrap: Named for the thin black line under its head, they nest in huge colonies on Antarctic islands.
Penguin species.Macaroni: Its yellow crest recalled the fashionable 'macaroni' dandies of 18th-century England, as in Yankee Doodle.
Penguin species.Rockhopper: It moves over rocky shores by hopping with both feet together; its yellow eyebrow plumes are unmistakable.
Penguin species.Magellanic: Named for Ferdinand Magellan, who saw them in 1520; they nest in burrows in Patagonia.
Penguin species.Humboldt: It lives on the Peruvian and Chilean coasts, cooled by the Humboldt Current that gave it its name.
Penguin species.Galapagos: The only penguin that lives partly north of the equator, on the Galapagos Islands.
Penguin species.Royal: Found only on Macquarie Island, near Australia, with orange crest plumes.
Penguin species.Little blue: The smallest penguin, around 33 cm tall; at dusk they parade up beaches at Phillip Island, Australia.
Penguin species.Puffin: Atlantic puffins can fly, beating their wings hundreds of times a minute, and live only in the north.
Penguin species.Razorbill: A close relative of the extinct great auk; it lives in the North Atlantic and flies.
Penguin species.Guillemot: A black-and-white northern seabird that looks penguin-like but flies; penguins are southern.
Penguin species.Great auk: A flightless North Atlantic bird hunted to extinction in the 1840s, and the original bird called 'penguin'.
Penguin species.Skua: An aggressive seabird that raids penguin colonies for eggs and chicks.
Penguin species.Albatross: A flying bird of the Southern Ocean, the wandering albatross, which has the longest wingspan of any bird.
Penguin species.Petrel: A tube-nosed seabird; storm petrels are said to be named for St Peter walking on water.
Penguin species.Cormorant: A fish-diver that dries its wings spread out, and flies, unlike penguins.
Penguin species.Gannet: A big seabird that plunge-dives from height for fish, and flies easily.
Penguin species.Fulmar: A tube-nosed flier that spits foul-smelling oil at predators.
Penguin species.Tern: The Arctic tern migrates from the Arctic to the Antarctic, possibly 70,000 km a year, the longest animal migration.
Penguin species.Murre: The North American name for some guillemots; they nest on cliffs and fly.

Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Macaque: The most widespread primate besides humans; Japan's snow monkeys bathe in hot springs to keep warm.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Baboon: Old World monkeys that live in troops that can number around 100 or more, with strict social hierarchies.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Capuchin: Named for the hood-like cap of hair that resembles Capuchin friars; they crack nuts with stone tools.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Howler monkey: Its roar is among the loudest of land animals, heard through dense forest from kilometers away.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Marmoset: Tiny monkeys that often give birth to twins, with fathers doing much of the carrying of the babies.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Tamarin: Emperor tamarins have a long white mustache said to resemble Kaiser Wilhelm II's.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Mandrill: The largest monkey, with males sporting vivid red-and-blue faces that grow brighter with status.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Colobus: Its name comes from the Greek for 'mutilated', since this African monkey lacks thumbs.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Squirrel monkey: This small monkey has one of the highest brain-to-body ratios among primates.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Spider monkey: A strong prehensile tail works like a fifth limb, with a sensitive bare tip for gripping branches.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Vervet: Uses different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, one of the best-studied animal vocabularies.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Proboscis monkey: A Borneo native and strong swimmer; males sport an enormous drooping nose used to attract mates.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Langur: Old World leaf-eating monkeys; Hanuman langurs are revered in Hindu tradition and roam many Indian towns.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Gorilla: The largest living primate and an ape, so it has no tail, unlike every monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Chimpanzee: Along with bonobos, humans' closest relatives, so an ape with no tail rather than a monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Orangutan: Its name means 'person of the forest' in Malay, and it is an ape with no tail.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Gibbon: A lesser ape that swings by brachiation and has no tail, so not a monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Bonobo: An ape, and together with chimpanzees our closest living relative, so not a monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Siamang: The largest gibbon, with an inflatable throat sac for loud calls; an ape, not a monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Lemur: Madagascar's primates are not monkeys but a separate, older branch of the primate family tree.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Tarsier: A tiny primate with enormous eyes, only a distant relative of monkeys, which is why it does not qualify.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Loris: The slow loris is among the few venomous mammals, and as a loris it is not a monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Aye-aye: This Madagascar lemur has a long thin finger for tapping wood to find grubs, and is no monkey.
Monkeys (not apes or lemurs).Human: We are apes, not monkeys, even though people often group us with the primates in the trees.

Disney animal characters.Simba: The name is Swahili for lion. The Lion King, in 1994, was also the first Disney animated film with an original story, not an adaptation.
Disney animal characters.Bambi: The deer comes from Felix Salten's 1923 Austrian novel, and Disney's 1942 film was inspired by the Maine woods.
Disney animal characters.Thumper: Bambi's rabbit friend gets his name from thumping his foot, and he says his mother taught him not to say anything if he cannot say something nice.
Disney animal characters.Dumbo: The 1941 elephant, whose giant ears let him fly, speaks no lines, and the film runs only about 64 minutes.
Disney animal characters.Baloo: The bear in The Jungle Book sang 'The Bare Necessities', and his name comes from Kipling's bhalu, Hindi for bear.
Disney animal characters.Pumbaa: The warthog's name is Swahili for foolish or simple. He and Timon are known for the motto 'Hakuna Matata'.
Disney animal characters.Timon: The meerkat in The Lion King shares his name with a Shakespeare play, Timon of Athens, but this is a coincidence.
Disney animal characters.Flounder: The Little Mermaid's fish friend is actually drawn like a tropical fish, not a flounder, which are flat.
Disney animal characters.Abu: Aladdin's monkey sidekick was voiced by Frank Welker, who also voiced Marcel in Friends.
Disney animal characters.Tramp: The mutt of Lady and the Tramp, 1955, in which the spaghetti-sharing scene is among the best-known moments in animation.
Disney animal characters.Bolt: The dog from Disney's 2008 film thinks his TV superpowers are real. It was one of the first Disney films released in 3D.
Disney animal characters.Basil: The mouse detective of The Great Mouse Detective, 1986, is modelled on Sherlock Holmes, and the film is based on Eve Titus's books.
Disney animal characters.Bugs Bunny: Famous for 'What's up, Doc?', he belongs to Warner Bros., not Disney.
Disney animal characters.Garfield: Jim Davis's lasagna-loving cat appeared in 1978 and was never a Disney character.
Disney animal characters.Scooby-Doo: The Great Dane is a Hanna-Barbera creation, first seen in 1969, with no link to Disney.
Disney animal characters.Snoopy: The Peanuts beagle was created by Charles Schulz, and he is not a Disney character.
Disney animal characters.Tom: The cat of Tom and Jerry is from MGM and Hanna-Barbera, and the series won seven Oscars.
Disney animal characters.Jerry: The mouse who outwits Tom is from MGM, not Disney, and he is a different mouse from Mickey.
Disney animal characters.Yogi Bear: He lives in Jellystone Park and is a Hanna-Barbera bear who is smarter than the average bear.
Disney animal characters.Daffy Duck: A Warner Bros. creation of 1937, he is sometimes confused with Donald Duck, but is not Disney.
Disney animal characters.Porky Pig: He signs off every cartoon with 'That's all, folks!' and is a Warner Bros. character.
Disney animal characters.Pink Panther: He first appeared in the opening credits of the 1963 film, and he is a creation of Friz Freleng, not Disney.
Disney animal characters.Road Runner: Chased by Wile E. Coyote, he is a Warner Bros. star who says 'meep meep', and he is no Disney character.
Disney animal characters.Tweety: The yellow canary is another Warner Bros. star who is always chased by Sylvester, and he is no Disney character.

Figures in the Exodus story.Moses: Raised in Pharaoh's household, he led the Israelites out of Egypt, and tradition credits him with receiving the Ten Commandments at Sinai.
Figures in the Exodus story.Aaron: Moses's older brother served as his spokesman before Pharaoh and became the first high priest of Israel.
Figures in the Exodus story.Miriam: Moses's sister watched over his basket on the Nile and later led the women in song and dance after the Red Sea crossing.
Figures in the Exodus story.Pharaoh: The Exodus text never names him, so which ruler it refers to, if any, remains debated by scholars.
Figures in the Exodus story.Zipporah: A Midianite priest's daughter, she became Moses's wife and, in one puzzling episode, circumcised their son to avert danger.
Figures in the Exodus story.Jethro: Moses's father-in-law, a priest of Midian, advised him to delegate judging disputes to capable officials instead of handling everything alone.
Figures in the Exodus story.Joshua: He led the Israelite fight against Amalek, accompanied Moses up Sinai, and later succeeded him in leading the people into Canaan.
Figures in the Exodus story.Hur: He and Aaron held up Moses's arms during the battle with Amalek so the Israelites kept winning.
Figures in the Exodus story.Bezalel: A craftsman said to be filled with divine skill, he was appointed to build the Tabernacle and the Ark of the Covenant.
Figures in the Exodus story.Amalek: The Amalekites attacked the weary Israelites at Rephidim, and the text says that Israel's memory of this attack was never to fade.
Figures in the Exodus story.Noah: Noah's flood belongs to Genesis, long before Exodus, so he is a trap among these Exodus figures.
Figures in the Exodus story.Abraham: Abraham is a Genesis patriarch, appearing centuries before the Exodus in the story's timeline.
Figures in the Exodus story.David: King David lived long after the Exodus, in the era of the monarchy, so he is not part of this story.
Figures in the Exodus story.Solomon: Solomon, David's son, built the Temple in Jerusalem, a project the Bible dates roughly 480 years after the Exodus.
Figures in the Exodus story.Samson: His story is in Judges, in the period after Joshua, so it falls well after the Exodus.
Figures in the Exodus story.Elijah: A prophet of the northern kingdom in the Books of Kings, centuries after Moses, famed for the Mount Carmel contest.
Figures in the Exodus story.Jonah: Jonah is the prophet swallowed by a great fish, a story told in his own short book, far from Exodus.
Figures in the Exodus story.Goliath: The Philistine giant fell to David's sling, well into the monarchy period and long after Exodus.
Figures in the Exodus story.Delilah: She appears in the Samson story in Judges, which is set well after the Exodus.
Figures in the Exodus story.Daniel: Daniel and the lions' den belongs to the Babylonian exile, about a thousand years after the Exodus tradition.
Figures in the Exodus story.Esther: Esther became queen of Persia and saved her people, a tale from the exile era, not Exodus.
Figures in the Exodus story.Ruth: The Moabite widow of the Book of Ruth lived in the time of the Judges and became an ancestor of King David.
Figures in the Exodus story.Gideon: A judge who defeated Midian with a tiny force, 300 men, he lived after the Exodus and the conquest of Canaan.
Figures in the Exodus story.Saul: The first king of Israel, anointed centuries after the Exodus events.
